articles.title: North Korea Expands Missiles and Drones With Russian Help
articles.body:
North Korea has advanced its ballistic missile systems and established mass production lines for strike drones with technical and operational assistance from Russia, The New York Times reported.
Moscow is transferring military technologies, telemetry feedback, and operational expertise to Pyongyang in exchange for North Korean ammunition, labor, and combat troops deployed in support of Russia’s war effort in Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In early October, North Korea conducted a test launch of a tactical ballistic missile that Pyongyang claimed is capable of delivering a nuclear warhead.
South Korean and Japanese defense tracking systems recorded the munition traveling approximately 700 kilometers (435 miles), whereas state media in Pyongyang asserted the missile achieved an operational flight range of 1,000 kilometers (621 miles).
Departing from routine diplomatic protocols that traditionally limit Seoul to brief statements of condemnation following Northern missile tests, South Korea conducted its first operational test of a domestically developed hypersonic ballistic missile five days later.
The test launch was observed in person by South Korean President Lee Jae-myung, reflecting growing institutional concern in Seoul regarding Pyongyang’s accelerated technological timeline.
Russian combat feedback, accuracy, and mass drone assembly
Western intelligence and defense analysts observe that Pyongyang is leveraging Russian operational data detailing how North Korean weapons perform in real combat environments against modern Western-supplied air defense systems.
Russian Drone Hits Vinnytsia Apartment Block, 6 Injured
Defense analyst Anton Ponomarenko noted that telemetry and performance feedback provided by the Russian military have enabled North Korean engineers to refine the guidance accuracy and terminal maneuverability of tactical ballistic missiles, increasing the conventional and nuclear strike risk posed to South Korea.
Concurrently, Moscow has assisted Pyongyang in establishing domestic industrial manufacturing lines for loitering munitions and strike drones.
Pyongyang has adapted lessons from the armed conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, where cost-effective unmanned platforms have repeatedly saturated and depleted advanced, high-cost air defense networks.
During North Korean military drills conducted last month, an integrated swarm of unmanned aerial vehicles conducted synchronized saturation strikes against an island target while cruise and ballistic missiles launched simultaneous strikes from multiple vectors.
Defense specialists emphasize that countering coordinated drone-swarm and missile saturation tactics could compel South Korea and its regional allies to overhaul integrated air and missile defense postures at substantial financial cost.
Expanding military alliance and troop deployments
The reciprocal technology transfers underscore the deepening military axis between Moscow and Pyongyang following the signing of a comprehensive strategic partnership agreement during Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to Pyongyang in June 2024, which codified a mutual defense clause.
In a birthday dispatch addressed to Putin on Oct. 7, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un reaffirmed “invariable support” for Moscow, characterizing Russia’s war in Ukraine as a “sacred war of justice” and pledging to expand bilateral strategic alignment.
The partnership encompasses significant conventional transfers and frontline force commitments. North Korea has supplied artillery munitions and ballistic missiles to the Russian military while deploying an estimated 14,000 to 15,000 military personnel to Russian, including roughly 10,000 combat infantry and 1,000 military engineers deployed in the Kursk region.
According to casualty assessments compiled by South Korea’s National Intelligence Service (NIS), approximately 6,000 North Korean soldiers deployed in support of Russian operations have been killed or wounded in combat, reinforcing Pyongyang’s reliance on Russian technological reciprocity to compensate for troop and material losses.

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1705: Starlink speed restored for Ukraine’s troops, Musk says SpaceX simply enforced its terms
articles.body:
Exclusives
Military
Ukraine strikes Russian plant supplying batteries for ballistic missiles and glide bombs with Storm Shadow missiles, OSINT reports – another hit on Russia’s weapons supply chain. The plant is reportedly Russia’s only producer of batteries for glide bomb guidance modules and a key supplier of specialized power sources for missile systems used in attacks on Ukraine.
Russian titanium plant in Urals reportedly hit by Ukrainian drones, 1,500 km from Ukraine. AVISMA, a major titanium producer in Russia’s Perm Krai, was reportedly hit by drones early on 25 October. The plant’s titanium alloys are used in military aircraft, engines, missiles, and space technology.
Ukrainian drones reportedly strike major shopping mall in Russia’s Belgorod overnight. Ukrainian forces reportedly struck the MegaGRINN shopping complex in Belgorod overnight, when it was closed.
Russian plant supplying components for Iskander missiles reportedly struck by Ukrainian Storm Shadow missiles. OSINT projects reported that a strike hit the Proton plant in Orel, a facility whose electronic components are used in several Russian weapons systems.
Drone strike sinks cargo ship near Romania, killing Ukrainian sailor. Romanian President blames Russia. The Khoryv capsized about 13 nautical miles off Romania’s coast, with nine crew members rescued and three still missing. The incident adds to a wave of attacks threatening Black Sea shipping and Ukraine’s export routes.
Denmark rushes 50,000 cannon rounds to Ukraine to help F-16s hunt Russia’s advanced jet drones. Ukrainian pilots are already using the 20-mm ammunition to intercept jet-powered attack drones, as Russia deploys faster targets that challenge Ukraine’s air defenses.
Ukraine wants partners’ Patriot interceptors now. Europe can hand them over only with US approval, Ukraine’s president says. Ukraine is contracting about 1,000 Patriot missiles that will take years to arrive, so it wants partners’ stocks today.
Intelligence and technology
Musk warns military use of Starlink could spark space war. Kyiv’s ex-disinformation chief says he’s building alibi after Starshield scandal. The warning lands weeks after his company throttled the Starshield service Ukraine’s drones rely on.
A modem from a Russian drone led reporters to its Chinese maker—which invoiced 500 for Russia’s drone plant. Posing as a Russian military supplier, journalists got a $2.87 million invoice, three bank accounts, and no pushback on military use.
Russia may stage sabotage in Eastern Europe, but wants Kyiv blamed, Ukraine’s Intelligence warns. The agency says Moscow aims to weaken European support for Kyiv by making Russian attacks appear to be the work of Ukraine’s military.
The money starts as bags of cash in a Moscow market and ends up clean in China, leaked files show. The firm, co-owned by the bank behind Russia’s defense industry, hides where the money starts before it reaches foreign banks.
The Starlink hot potato: Musk points to Trump, Trump points to nobody, then credits Musk with the fix. The speed limit stays. Ukraine’s military Starlink terminals still lose connection above about 160 km/h, nine days after the limit took effect, and Kyiv has no official explanation of who imposed it.
International
40,000 tons of Russian diesel are bound for New York—due four days after Americans vote. The tanker loaded at a Baltic port Ukrainian drones struck in March. Trump wants cheaper diesel before the midterms.
Russia’s attacks on Black Sea shipping raise risk of global famine, German FM warns. As Russian strikes increasingly threaten civilian vessels and Ukrainian grain exports, Germany’s foreign minister warned that shipping disruptions could leave vulnerable countries without essential food and fertilizers.
Austria expels Russian Embassy and OSCE diplomats over suspected spying. Vienna remains a Russian spy hub. Austrian security authorities raised suspicions of espionage involving four Russian diplomats, prompting Vienna to declare them persona non grata.
Russian Geran drone crashes in Moldova near homes and energy facility: Chisinau expels Russian diplomat. President Maia Sandu condemned the latest incursion as Russia’s war on Ukraine increasingly threatens neighboring Moldova.
Finland gives Ukraine 10 diesel locomotives that keep trains running when Russian strikes cut the power. The engines come free from Finland’s state railway, part of a visit that also brought winter energy money and new defense, housing, and satellite deals for Kyiv.
45 seconds of voting in the Lviv Oblast Council sparked a new dispute with Poland: Warsaw says Kyiv promised the UPA year decision will not take effect. Poland is Ukraine’s main hub for Western aid, and every new fight over the two nations’ WWII past erodes the trust that role rests on.
Humanitarian and social impact
Pope’s envoy becomes first foreign representative to gain access to Ukrainian POWs held by Russia since 2022. Cardinal Matteo Zuppi, Pope Leo XIV’s special envoy, was allowed to physically visit Ukrainian prisoners of war held by Russia during his recent visit, Ukrainian ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said.
Ceasefire planned for occupied Oleshky as residents face starvation and blocked escape routes, White House announces. A truce announced by Melania Trump is due to take effect October 29, opening the way for humanitarian supplies and evacuations if Russia and Ukraine implement the agreement.
Ukraine frees 270 from Russian captivity in “historic” prisoner swap, including 5 Olenivka survivors and American teacher Stephen Hubbard. The latest exchange returned 261 military personnel and nine civilians. Some had been held since 2018, while many others were captured during the defense of Mariupol in 2022.
Russia has kept the Red Cross away from Ukrainian POWs since 2024. Now about 1,500 captives it never confirmed as prisoners face prosecution. A captive soldier’s wife says that whenever families find a relative, Russia moves them to another prison and contact is lost again.
Political and legal developments
US midterms could restore Ukraine’s American aid and curb Trump’s Russia deals, if Democrats win Congress. Trump waives sanctions on Moscow that Congress wrote into law. Democrats could fight back after 3 November.
Putin claims Russia is ready for new talks with Ukraine, calls occupied land historical Russia. He also cited unnamed genetic studies to claim Russians and Ukrainians are one people, a day after hosting a US envoy.
Russia keeps hitting Ukraine’s arms plants. Now private developers can dig them space underground—and sell or rent it to them. The state budget has paid to keep war-damaged arms plants running. The new model brings private money into the digging.

articles.title: Saudi downs 10 Houthi missiles as Riyadh airport reopens
articles.body:
The New Arab's live blog is now closed. Here were the top stories:
Saudi Arabia has downed 10 Houthi ballistic missiles and a drone fired against the capital, Riyadh, according to the Saudi-led coalition supporting the internationally recognised Yemeni government. Explosions were heard in Riyadh, according to AFP.
King Khalid International Airport has reopened terminals one and two following Houthi missile strikes in early October that killed 17 people and wounded over 330. Terminals three and four, which were struck by the Houthis, are yet to reopen.
Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi is warning that any Israeli and US attack will not change the country's position, saying at an event in Tehran: "Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same."
The US embassy in Riyadh has announced that it has ordered non-emergency staffers and family members to leave Saudi Arabia, citing continued attacks by Yemen's Houthis against the country.
Security Alert: U.S. Mission Saudi Arabia (October 25, 2026) Effective October 23, 2026, the Department of State ordered non-emergency U.S. government employees and U.S. government employee family members to leave Saudi Arabia due to safety risks. Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions. The hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area. U.S. government employees working in Saudi Arabia require special authorization from Chief of Mission to use any airport in Saudi Arabia following recent missile and UAV attacks on airports in the Kingdom. King Khalid International Airport (RUH) in Riyadh announced a partial reopening as of October 25 for domestic flights and some international flights operated by national carriers. A limited number of flights normally based at RUH are operating out of Qassim-based Prince Naif bin Abdulaziz International Airport (ELQ). Operations at King Abdulaziz International Airport in Jeddah (JED) are operational with some delays and cancellations. Operations at King Fahd International Airport in Dammam (DMM) are operational with some delays and cancellations. U.S. citizens should be aware of potential attacks on airports, airspace closures, flight cancellations, and travel disruptions. Please take extreme caution if you choose to use airports in Saudi Arabia. We recommend checking your flight departure status directly with the airline and with the airport. Read more: https://t.co/Vgg95JTPsw
The commander of US Central Command (CENTCOM) has visited the Strait of Hormuz, saying a statement that the visit "underscores our strong commitment to continued freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz."
"Today, primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz remain free and clear of Iranian sea mines thanks to incredible efforts by our people," he said, adding that "we remain intensely focused on keeping commercial traffic flowing as we work with our teammates in the U.S. interagency, Gulf Cooperation Council, and shipping industry."
The visit comes amid tension between the US, Iran and Israel, as reports in US media continue to emerge of renewed preparations made by the US to strike Iran.
Sri Lanka coordinated the rescue of 40 Iranian sailors from multiple commercial ships in international waters off the coast of the country and supported their return to Iran, a spokesman for the island nation's foreign ministry said on Sunday.
The ministry received a request from the Iranian embassy via diplomatic channels to rescue the sailors, Thushara Rodrigo, a spokesman for the ministry, said, adding they had been suffering unspecified medical emergencies.
The ministry didn't give any further details of why they had to be rescued but local media including Indian national newspaper The Hindu reported they were on board vessels which were US-sanctioned oil tankers.
Washington has imposed a blockade on Iranian shipping as part of its war on Iran.
The sailors from 19 ships were brought ashore at Galle Harbour, about 126 km from commercial capital Colombo, and were given medical treatment before returning to Iran early on Sunday morning, the spokesman added.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that Iran and its allies might try to disrupt Tuesday's Israeli elections, warning the Islamic Republic against any hostile acts.
The premier has campaigned heavily on his security credentials, touting the war he launched against Iran in February alongside the United States and suggesting that he alone can see it through.
"We have intelligence signs that our enemies, Iran and its proxies, could challenge us with attacks in order to disrupt the elections," Netanyahu said in a video released by his office on Sunday.
"Don't test us. You will suffer disproportionate blows," he added, noting the military was ready for both defensive and offensive operations.
Earlier in the day, the premier posted an AI-generated image of a mushroom cloud engulfing Tel Aviv, alongside text attributed to a right-wing political commentator calling Iran an existential threat and arguing that all the other issues discussed this election season were trivial in comparison.
The image was labelled as fearmongering by his opposition rivals.
The 2027 edition of the Dakar Rally has been moved out of Saudi Arabia due to security concerns, organisers Amaury Sport Organisation said on Sunday.
The event, due to take place in January and which has been held in Saudi Arabia since 2020, wouldmove to a different territory, with the location to be announced in the coming days, the ASO said in a statement.
Reuters reported on Wednesday that the Dakar Rally wouldtake place in Africa, citing sources involved in the World Rally-Raid Championship.
"Amaury Sport Organisation and Saudi Motorsport Company have jointly decided that Dakar Saudi Arabia 2027, scheduled from 1 to 15 January, 2027, will not be held in the Kingdom, following recent developments in the region," the ASO said.
Qatari mediators were in Tehran on Sunday as part of an effort to de-escalate regional tensions in coordination with the United States, an official briefed on the situation told Reuters.
An Israeli strike on a university in Gaza City killed three people on Sunday, staff and a local hospital said, while the civil defence agency reported four others killed elsewhere in the territory.
Al Shifa hospital said it received three bodies and treated eight people who were wounded in the Gaza City drone strike, with two sources at the Islamic University saying those killed were administrative staff and the injured were students.
Gaza's education ministry said in a statement that the students had been present for classes.
It went on to condemn the strike and said "the global silence regarding attacks on students and universities serves as encouragement for the continuation of these crimes".
"This strike occurs at a time when the higher education sector is facing total annihilation, with 95 percent of the buildings belonging to academic institutions having been damaged as a result of the war," it continued.
"This heinous assault is part of a continuous series of attacks on education; over the past six days, 10 students and educators have been killed by the occupation's fire."
More than 100 economists, including former Bank of Israel officials, ex-central bank governor Jacob Frenkel and several Nobel laureates, signed a letter expressing alarm over Netanyahu's proposed crypto plan, saying it would lead to higher unemployment, a fall in foreign investment and the collapse of Israel's economic standing in the world.
In an interview with Israel's Channel 10 on Friday, Netanyahu said he was preparing for a scenario in which broader sanctions were imposed on Israel.
"There could be sanctions, and sanctions on banks so you need to set up a bypass economy," Netanyahu said. "You know, there are currencies that can bypass (sanctions). We are also working on that."
In response to Netanyahu's comments, the letter read: "As we have seen in countries that have suffered similar sanctions, such as South Africa, Iran, and Russia, the living standards of Israeli citizens would plummet dramatically, and the state's ability to finance its security and defend itself against its enemies would be severely damaged."
"Netanyahu is knowingly leading the State of Israel toward boycott and international economic isolation, and all he has to offer the Israeli economy is a puzzling solution, one accepted in criminal organisations, that will not help in the slightest."
Israeli forces have demolished Palestinian homes and businesses in Hebron and forcibly displaced around 2,500 people, according to Palestinian rights monitors, as a sweeping military crackdown entered its third day on Sunday with further raids and arrests across the southern occupied West Bank.
Bulldozers have torn through residential and commercial areas, with footage showing homes reduced to rubble across several blocks. The demolitions follow Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's threat to destroy the neighbourhood from which two Palestinian gunmen allegedly came after an attack on an Israeli military checkpoint on Friday.
The Palestinian Centre for Human Rights (PCHR), citing preliminary estimates from Hebron municipality, said approximately 500 families comprising around 2,500 people had been forced from their homes in an area spanning 350 dunums, or 35 hectares. Israeli forces have sealed the area and continued house searches, leaving displaced residents uncertain when they will be allowed to return.
The operation has targeted Ein Deir Baha and surrounding neighbourhoods, alongside homes, businesses and industrial facilities in Farsh al-Hawa.
PCHR documented the demolition of a three-storey house, a commercial facility selling car parts and the walls surrounding a tile and ceramics business's yard. The organisation said the house was demolished despite its owner having obtained an interim court order following an earlier demolition notice.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has published a photo of a nuclear strike on Tel Aviv as a warning in the event he is not reelected as PM, a move opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot described as 'fearmongering'
In the post made on X, Netanyahu says that "if the Iranians obtain nuclear weapons, nothing else will matter anymore," including the controversies around his premiership, such as allowing the evasion of the Ultra-Orthodox draft, adding that Israeli voters should vote for a candidate that can "complete the mission" or expose the country to a "second holocaust."
Netanyahu also went on to warn that finishing the job against Iran would not happen by a candidate that requires the support of "Muslim Brotherhood and terror enablers", a reference to Israel's Palestinian parties that could be well placed to determine the next government, as both Netanyahu and Opposition blocs poll under the 61-seat threshold to form a government.
Palestinian parties have consistently been used as a scare tactic in the election to warn against votes for Eisenkot's coalition.
Eisenkot responded by calling Netanyahu "hysterical", adding that "as in every election campaign, it's the same method of lies and scare tactics. This time, threatening Israeli citizens with mass destruction. And this is after you failed to achieve the objectives of the war in Iran."
Democrats head Yair Golan, part of Eisenkot's bloc, also responded, saying: "On Tuesday, we will replace those who sow panic and restore security and sanity to Israel."
Saudi Arabia issued danger warnings, which have since passed, for the Jazan and Taif regions of the country, as Yemen's Houthis continue to launch ballistic missiles and drones against the country.
Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Sunday called for a campaign to cut gas consumption by at least 10 percent, with officials anticipating shortages as winter approaches.
While a major producer, Iran has long suffered shortages of natural gas, essential for powering heating systems, which have been exacerbated by war with the United States and Israel that began in February.
During the most intense phase of the fighting, which lasted nearly 40 days, the two countries struck key Iranian infrastructure, including natural gas refineries, according to Tehran.
Winter in Iran often sees temperatures drop below freezing, especially in the country's north.
"To get through the approaching winter, a nationwide effort is essential ... to reduce gas consumption by at least 10 percent," said Ghalibaf in a video carried by Iranian media.
"Anyone who saves gas, regardless of the amount, will immediately receive the corresponding proceeds in their bank account, allowing everyone to see the tangible impact of those savings on their household budget."
Tehran strikes Iranian Kurdish base in Iraq with drones
Iran's armed forces attacked bases belonging to an Iranian Kurdish opposition group in Iraq's Kurdistan region using drones, a media outlet in Tehran reported on Sunday.
"As part of a drone operation carried out by the Revolutionary Guards' ground forces, the headquarters of the terrorist and separatist group Komala, located in the Balisan region, was targeted last night," the Mehr news agency said.
The semi-autonomous region hosts camps and bases belonging to several groups of Iranian Kurdish militants, which Iran has targeted repeatedly since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in February.
The Revolutionary Guards have not immediately claimed responsibility for the strikes on these fighters, whom Iran accuses of being supported by Israel, its sworn enemy.
In the most deadly recent attack, nine Komala members were killed on 17 July near the city of Sulaymaniyah.
The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition announced that it has intercepted 10 ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis against Saudi Arabia's southern region.

Iran’s air defence systems shot down a US LUCAS drone over the southern port city of Bandar Abbas, the Iranian army said on Sunday, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that a potential resumption of war with Israel and the United States would not change his country's position.
The remarks come amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, as President Donald Trump said on Friday that Washington "may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the US-Israeli campaign on Iran that began on 28 February.
"Recently, there has been talk of a new war, but I am already thinking about the post-war period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same," said Araghchi during a televised event in Tehran.
"They have already done so twice and have seen the results. If they want to try again, they know they will achieve no different outcome from those of the past."
An April 8 ceasefire between Iran and the United States put an end to the most intense fighting, apart from sporadic exchanges of fire in and around the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies.

articles.title: U.S. to Ban Chinese BYD Vehicles from Japan Air Base
articles.body:
The U.S. military will ban Chinese BYD vehicles from entering Kadena Air Base in Japan over concerns about potential leaks of military secrets.
The Japanese publication Kangnam Times reported the decision.
The restrictions will apply not only to privately owned vehicles but also to contractors’ vehicles, taxis, delivery vehicles, and commercial transport. If such a vehicle arrives at the base’s gate, the driver will be ordered to turn around immediately.
Kadena Air Base is one of the U.S. Air Force’s major overseas installations and plays a key role in Japan’s defense andAmerica’s security strategy in the Indo-Pacific region.
Kadena Air Base is home to the U.S. Air Force’s 18th Wing of the Fifth Air Force, which includes KC-135 aerial refueling tankers, E-3 Sentry airborne early warning and control aircraft, and HH-60W search-and-rescue helicopters. F-35A, F-22A, and F-16C fighter jets are also deployed to the base on a rotational basis.
The base also hosts the Typhon missile system, which can launch Tomahawk cruise missiles for strikes against ground targets or long-range SM-6 missiles capable of intercepting both aerodynamic targets and ballistic missiles.
The aim of the new restrictions is to prevent the collection of military intelligence using vehicles. Modern electric vehicles are equipped with cameras and various sensors that gather information about their surroundings, and their functions increasingly rely on software. This creates risks of data leaks involving the locations of military facilities and details of their operations.
According to the publication, officials are also discussing the possibility of extending the ban to other U.S. military bases. Similar measures could be introduced not only at other U.S. facilities in Japan, including Marine Corps Air Station Futenma on Okinawa, but also at U.S. military bases in South Korea.
The U.S. has previously imposed restrictions on Chinese equipment. In 2018, the Pentagon banned the sale of Huawei and ZTE smartphones, modems, and other equipment at stores on U.S. military bases worldwide due to information security risks.
In January 2025, the U.S. Department of Commerce approved restrictions on importing and selling vehicles equipped with certain software and hardware originating from China or Russia. The software restrictions will take effect for model year 2027 vehicles, while the hardware restrictions will apply to model year 2030 vehicles.
In early October, Norwegian military personnel discovered that rented Chinese vehicles were automatically recording and storing video footage during military exercises.
The Norwegian Armed Forces use rental vehicles from First Rent A Car Norway AS, which operates under the Hertz brand, for day-to-day activities, training exercises, and operational tasks. The company is part of the Volvo Cars corporate structure, whose majority owner is China’s Zhejiang Geely Holding Group.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Starshield operations restored to normal speed, Zelensky confirms as Elon Musk claims Ukraine violated Starlink terms
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Starshield operations restored to normal speed, Zelensky confirms as Elon Musk claims Ukraine violated Starlink terms
Key developments on Oct. 24-25:
- Starshield operations restored to normal speed, Zelensky confirms as Elon Musk claims Ukraine violated Starlink terms
- Russian attacks kill 8, injure 51 across Ukraine over past day as drone strikes residential building in Vinnytsia
- Moscow ready to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine, US after Nov. 4, Kremlin aide says
- In less than 24 hours, Russia hits 4 hypermarkets belonging to one of Ukraine's largest retail chains
- Massive Ukrainian drone attack hits shopping center in Russia's Belgorod Oblast, locals say
Starshield operations restored to normal speed, Zelensky confirms as Elon Musk claims Ukraine violated Starlink terms
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that Starlink and Starshield, the militarized version of Elon Musk's satellite internet system, Starlink, was working at full speed as of the morning of Oct. 24, after it had previously been limited to 161 kilometers per hour (about 100 miles per hour).
"The speeds are now where they need to be," Zelensky said. "I thank all Americans and all our partners who took this seriously and truly helped us. I thank members of Congress, senators, all the media, the State Department, and the President."
Ukraine's Defense Ministry told reporters on Oct. 24 that Starshield was working above speeds of 400 kilometers per hour (about 248 miles per hour) again.
"We record a speed of more than 400 kilometers per hour, the connection is stable," the ministry said.
The ministry continues to monitor and record the work of Starlink and Starshield, according to Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara.
"This is another example of direct dialogue and the persistent position of the President of Ukraine at the highest level yielding results. And this result is, above all, important for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics, and communications," the ministry added.
Musk later said that Ukraine's military violated the terms of service for Starlink, adding that the "loophole" has now been closed.
Ukraine's "military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week," he said in a post to X.
"Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately. This is not a threat, it is simply a statement of fact," Musk said.
He also claimed that SpaceX has done more than any other company to help Ukraine in its fight against Russia's war.
Ukrainian activist and former Defense Ministry adviser Serhii Sternenko denied that Ukraine violated Starlink's terms of service.
"As someone who was inside the process at the Ministry of Defense, I can say with certainty that this is not true. In February of this year, whitelists were introduced. Stationary terminals could be registered by both military personnel and civilians," he said in a post to X.
"But for any satellite terminal to work while on the move, it had to be added to a special list and connected to the military Starshield system. Otherwise, no satellite communication terminals in Ukraine would work," Sternenko added.
Using Starlink for drone missions has been "technically impossible" since all drone campaigns that require satellite communications would only work with the military Starshield service, he said.
Presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov also denied Musk's claims, saying that all Starlink terminals operating in Ukraine have a speed restriction of 70-90 kilometers an hour and do not work on Russian territory.
"Thus, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and medium-range strikes," he said in a post to Facebook. "It is very strange that Elon Musk is not aware of Starlink restrictions in Ukraine."

Russian attacks kill 8, injure 51 across Ukraine over past day as drone strikes residential building in Vinnytsia
Russian attacks killed eight people and injured 51 others across Ukraine over the past day, local authorities said on Oct. 24-25.
A Russian drone struck a five-story residential building in the city of Vinnytsia overnight on Oct. 25, injuring six people, one of whom was hospitalized, Nataliia Zabolotna, head of the Vinnytsia Oblast Military Administration, said.
The strike caused structural damage between the second and third floors, completely destroying four apartments and damaging nearby parked cars, Zabolotna added.
Alongside attacks on Vinnytsia, Russia launched 153 Shahed-type drones at Ukraine overnight on Oct. 25, including 92 jet-powered drones, as well as low-cost Banderol cruise missiles, the Ukrainian Air Force said.
Ukrainian air defenses intercepted 119 drones, including 64 jet-powered ones. As of 8 a.m., efforts to intercept the remaining drones were ongoing, with at least nine still in Ukrainian airspace.
Some drones evaded Ukrainian air defenses and struck 15 locations, while falling debris was recorded at nine other locations, according to the Air Force.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Russian attacks on the Synelnykove District on Oct. 24 killed three people and injured 14 others, including an 11-year-old girl, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said. Five of the injured were hospitalized in serious condition.
In the Nikopol District, Russian attacks over the past day killed two women and injured five people, including a 14-year-old boy, Hanzha added.
In Kharkiv Oblast, Russian attacks killed a 45-year-old man in the town of Lozova and injured two other men, aged 43 and 26, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
In Kharkiv, a 39-year-old man was injured. Russian attacks also wounded three men, aged 70, 54, and 47, in the town of Derhachi, and a 45-year-old woman in the village of Mala Danylivka, Syniehubov added.
In Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks killed one person in the village of Yarova and injured six others elsewhere in the region, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In Sumy Oblast, a 31-year-old woman was killed in a Russian attack on a farm in the Buryn community, which also injured an 18-year-old man. In the Boromlia community, a Russian drone struck a car, injuring three women aged 68, 56, and 36, according to local authorities.
Russian attacks injured four people in Zaporizhzhia Oblast over the past day. Russian forces carried out 832 strikes on 52 settlements across the region using drones, artillery, aircraft, and multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS), local authorities said.
In Kherson Oblast, Russian attacks targeted 43 settlements, including the regional center of Kherson, injuring two people, Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said.
In Chernihiv Oblast, two women suffered acoustic trauma in a Russian strike on the regional capital, Chernihiv, on Oct. 24, Governor Viacheslav Chaus said.
One person was injured in a Russian drone attack on Kyiv on Oct. 24, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.

Moscow ready to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine, US after Nov. 4, Kremlin aide says
The Kremlin is ready to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine and the U.S. after Nov. 4, when Russia celebrates National Unity Day, Russian President Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov told state-controlled outlet Vesti on Oct. 25.
The statement follows Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's Oct. 23 remarks that a new round of trilateral talks is expected in the first half of November, with Abu Dhabi a possible venue.
"The next deadline is now Nov. 4, our major holiday. After that, we will be ready to resume negotiations," Ushakov said.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected ceasefire proposals, demanding instead that Kyiv cede the only partially occupied Donbas, a strategically important region in eastern Ukraine. Such a concession would give Moscow territory that Russian forces have been unable to capture on the battlefield. Ukraine, in contrast, has agreed to multiple ceasefire proposals put forward by the U.S.
Ushakov said he did not expect the first trilateral meeting after the pause to yield significant results, calling it a "trial run." A peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine "still needs work," he added.
On Oct. 20, U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European partners, including Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store.
The following day, Witkoff held a three-hour meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, after which the Kremlin said it was ready to resume trilateral talks in November.
Witkoff said on Oct. 21 that discussions among Ukrainian, U.S., and Russian representatives would "continue at the technical level."
Putin has long avoided meeting with Zelensky. Instead, the Kremlin chief is reportedly seeking a meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump in China next month in an effort to secure a favorable peace deal without Ukraine's participation.
In recent weeks, Trump has also lashed out at Zelensky, unilaterally announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine that ultimately failed, threatened to cut off intelligence-sharing with Kyiv, and eased sanctions on Russian oil exports.
Trump has defended the sanctions relief, arguing that it could encourage Moscow to take part in peace negotiations with Kyiv.

articles.title: Ukraine strikes Russian titanium plant more than 1,400 kilometers from border, monitoring channel claims
articles.body:
Ukraine strikes Russian titanium plant, facility producing missile, drone components, monitoring channels claim
Editor's note: This story was updated to include details of a reported Ukrainian attack on Lipetsk Oblast.
Ukrainian forces struck Avisma, one of the world's largest titanium sponge producers in Russia's Perm Krai, and the Energiya plant in Lipetsk Oblast, which manufactures components for missile systems and drones, on Oct. 25, Ukrainian and Russian monitoring channels reported.
Perm Krai Governor Dmitry Makhonin said at around 11 a.m. local time that 11 drones had been downed during a Ukrainian attack on the region.
Makhonin added that an "industrial facility" in the northern part of the region had sustained "minor" damage but continued to operate as normal. The governor did not specify which facility had been damaged.
According to Makhonin, five employees of the facility were also injured in the Ukrainian attack.
Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ said the strike targeted Avisma in the town of Berezniki, located about 170 kilometers (105 miles) from the regional center of Perm. The plant is part of Russian metallurgical corporation VSMPO-AVISMA.
Located more than 1,400 kilometers (870 miles) from the Ukrainian-Russian border, Avisma has been under U.S. sanctions since 2023. The plant manufactures products used in military aircraft, nuclear submarines, armored vehicles, and missile systems.
Later in the day, Ukrainian forces also attacked the Energiya plant in the city of Yelets, in Russia's Lipetsk Oblast, more than 200 kilometers (120 miles) from the Ukrainian border, the Russian independent media outlet Astra reported, citing open-source intelligence (OSINT) data.
Lipetsk Oblast Governor Igor Artamonov said an "industrial zone" had been targeted, injuring one person. The governor did not identify the facility that came under attack.
Energiya is Russia's largest research and production enterprise specializing in electrochemical power sources. Its products are used across various sectors, including the defense industry, civil aviation, maritime transport and energy. The plant manufactures batteries for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), power sources for air defense missile systems, and batteries for aircraft and naval vessels.
The enterprise is under sanctions imposed by the U.S., the European Union, the U.K., Canada, Switzerland, Japan, Australia and Ukraine.
The plant was previously attacked in May and July 2025, as well as in January 2026.
Ukraine had not commented on the reported strikes in Lipetsk Oblast and Perm Krai at the time of publication.
Ukraine regularly strikes military targets deep within Russia and occupied territories in an effort to diminish Moscow's ability to continue waging its war.
Ukraine's General Staff said Ukrainian forces also struck Russian military radar stations in Belgorod Oblast overnight on Oct. 25, as well as a Russian command post in occupied Zaporizhzhia Oblast and a command-and-observation post in occupied Kherson Oblast.
Other targets included concentrations of Russian troops in the occupied parts of Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia oblasts, the General Staff added.
Earlier, Ukrainian monitoring channels reported a fire at the Omsky Kauchuk petrochemical plant in the Russian city of Omsk following a Ukrainian attack.
The overnight attack on Belgorod also damaged a local shopping and entertainment center, monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported.
Belgorod Mayor Valentin Demidov said one person was killed and 10 others were injured in the attack. Residential buildings and cars were also damaged, he added.

Strikes on oil refineries and dozens of Russian vessels: how the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ secret unit operates
Kyiv • UNN
The Kairos unit was transformed into the 7th Separate Center with hundreds of military personnel. It coordinates long-range strikes on Russian targets.
The Ukrainian Kairos battalion, which participates in long-range strikes against Russian facilities, has been deployed within the 7th Separate Center of the Armed Forces of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces. This was reported by Bloomberg, according to UNN.
Details
According to the agency, the Kairos unit, which was previously part of the 414th Separate Brigade of Unmanned Systems “Magyar’s Birds,” has evolved into a much larger military structure. The 7th Separate Center now numbers hundreds of service members and is capable of coordinating operations by other units.
The commander of the formation, known by the call sign “Ray,” told journalists that the capabilities of Ukraine’s long-range strikes have grown significantly. Whereas previously drones could carry out missions at a distance of about 100 kilometers and carry a relatively small warhead, Ukrainian forces now use significantly more powerful weapons, including relatively inexpensive cruise missiles.
One of Kairos’s areas of activity has been attacks on Russian maritime logistics. According to the commander, over the course of one month the unit struck 60 vessels in the Sea of Azov. In addition, during the summer campaign aimed at isolating occupied Crimea, the Unmanned Systems Forces carried out approximately 7,000 strikes using drones. These figures were provided by the Ukrainian side; there has been no independent confirmation of all the claimed results.
Bloomberg also reports on Kairos’s involvement in large-scale attacks on Russian energy facilities. In particular, the unit took part in an operation to attack the territory of the Moscow oil refinery in Kapotnya on September 20, 2026. Following the attack, the facility suspended oil refining, and repairs to the damaged equipment could take several weeks.
Satellite reconnaissance and data analysis play an important role in preparing long-range strikes. Ukrainian forces use current and archival satellite imagery to study Russian facilities. Specialists with experience in the energy sector are also involved in planning the operations.
According to the agency’s assessment, the expansion of the capabilities of Ukrainian long-range strike units demonstrates significant changes in the conduct of the war. Ukraine is increasingly using its own technologies, intelligence data, and coordinated operations to strike Russia’s military and energy infrastructure at a considerable distance from the front line.

Long-range strike drones struck the “Avisma” titanium and chemical-metallurgical plant in the city of Berezniki in Russia’s Perm region overnight into Sunday, Oct. 25, targeting one of the world’s largest titanium production facilities, The Moscow Times and independent monitoring groups reported.
The enterprise operates as a subsidiary production division of VSMPO-Avisma Corporation, the world’s leading manufacturer of titanium sponge, specialized titanium alloys, and raw magnesium.

Perm Region Governor Dmitry Makhonin acknowledged the aerial incursion on Sunday, stating that an industrial enterprise situated in the northern sector of the province sustained “minor damage” following an attack by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
Makhonin claimed that the damaged facility continues to operate under standard routines and reported no casualties.
However, Ukrainian open-source intelligence (OSINT) monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported that the drone strikes engaged the production grounds of the Avisma chemical-metallurgical facility in Berezniki.
Local residents similarly reported hearing multiple drone engines followed by detonations and the sound of air defense engagements in the vicinity of the plant’s industrial perimeter.
Strategic defense metallurgy and aerospace components
The Berezniki metallurgical complex functions as an irreplaceable industrial node within the Russian Federation’s defense-industrial supply chain.
Trump Eyes Post-War Business Ties With Both Ukraine and Russia
Avisma specializes in the chemical processing of ilmenite ore into titanium tetrachloride and the subsequent thermal reduction of titanium sponge, alongside refining metallic magnesium and magnesium-based master alloys.
The refined titanium sponge and intermediate billets produced at Berezniki are transported to VSMPO’s primary smelting and mechanical processing facilities in Verkhnyaya Salda, Sverdlovsk region, to manufacture high-strength forgings, rolled sheets, and structural sub-assemblies.
The enterprise’s titanium alloys are critical structural materials utilized across Russian aerospace manufacturing, combat aviation, jet engine production, and missile systems.
Components fabricated from Avisma’s metals are integrated into fuselage airframes and turbine components for Su-35 and Su-57 fighter aircraft, fuselage mountings for tactical bombers, heavy armor assemblies, and missile airframes for cruise and ballistic platforms.
Beyond conventional defense hardware, specialized titanium castings and corrosion-resistant alloys from VSMPO-Avisma are supplied directly to Roscosmos for space rocket propulsion casings and to naval shipyards constructing nuclear-powered submarines.
Deep-tier asymmetric campaign against defense suppliers
The strike in Berezniki – located approximately 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from Ukrainian borders in the Ural Mountains – forms part of an expanding Ukrainian asymmetric campaign systematically targeting Russia’s deep-rear defense metallurgy and strategic chemical supply lines.
The incident in Perm region coincides with long-range drone strikes conducted across Siberia on Saturday, where unmanned platforms struck the Omsky Kauchuk chemical enterprise in Omsk – over 2,500 kilometers from Ukraine – igniting a large-scale blaze at a facility supplying synthetic rubbers and chemical binders used in solid rocket propellant for Iskander-M and intercontinental ballistic missile platforms.
Concurrently overnight into Sunday, Ukrainian strike drones engaged industrial and logistics infrastructure in central Belgorod, damaging the closed MegaGRINN commercial facility, while previous precision missile and drone interdictions hit the Proton defense microelectronics plant in Oryol and the Tolyattikauchuk petrochemical plant in Samara region.

articles.title: Musk warns military use of Starlink could spark space war. Kyiv’s ex-disinformation chief says he’s building alibi after Starshield scandal
articles.body:
SpaceX founder Elon Musk says that if Ukraine fires through Starlink, Russia would be entitled to shoot the network down. That is why Starlink must remain a civilian operation and cannot be used for outright offensive strikes that would put its very existence at risk.
The warning lands in the middle of a fight over Musk’s own hand on that network. Weeks ago, his company unexpectedly throttled the service Ukraine’s drones depend on amid US President Donald Trump diesel deal with Russia, which led to the disruption of a few operations on the front.
The US Treasury authorized the sale, delivery, offloading, and import of Russian-origin diesel fuel, effectively suspending sanctions on that trade until 7 April 2027, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) said on its website on 9 October.
The diesel deal combining intelligence halt and military Starlink, with pressure on Ukraine to make a quick peace deal, has angered both Democrats and Republicans ahead of the US elections on 3 November, where Democrats could win.
Meanwhile, a Ukrainian official interprets Musk's talk of strikes as an attempt to build an alibi before a possible investigation into that decision.
A civilian network, or a target
Musk was responding to a post warning that if Starlink shifted from a civilian network into a military system, Russia could treat it as a target for retaliation, and that destroying satellites in orbit could scatter enough debris to make space unusable for years or centuries.
“An adversary blowing up Starlink satellites would create a domino effect of destruction that would generate a vast field of debris, making space unusable," he writes.
When the shield and the warnings failed together
Overnight into 14 October, SpaceX quietly capped the speed of Starshield, the military version Ukraine’s drones run on, without telling Kyiv. Ukrainian units said the limit broke a series of missions, with connections dropping mid-flight and leaving drones hard to control.
At the same time, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine relies on the network for air defense, not attack, to intercept the Russian drones Moscow sends to its cities, and that once the speed was cut, his forces could no longer stop some of them as effectively as before.
Simultaneously, Ukraine's other American lifeline also went dark: for about three days, the US stopped passing the intelligence that warns of Russian ballistic launches. On 12 October, Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before the air-raid alert reached people, with no advance data from partners. In a strike during that window, three people were killed in the capital, the sirens sounding only after the blasts.
A Ukrainian official sees alibi-building
Meanwhile, Andrii Kovalenko, the ex-head of Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation, read Musk’s statement as self-protection rather than physics
“Musk, having taken responsibility for the restrictions on Starlink and Starshield for Ukraine, is now trying to build himself an alibi before a possible investigation into that decision,” he wrote.
He said that regardless of who was behind the idea of restricting Starlink and Starshield access for Ukraine, it represents a strategic setback for the US in the long run, as it risks portraying the country as an unreliable partner that may fail to honor its commitments.
"Europe purchases around 60% of its imported weapons from the US. Trust in the US as a security guarantor directly supports sales for American defense companies. Moves like this only undermine that trust and encourage European countries to develop their own systems," he said.
The US has sent a message that its guarantees may not be reliable and that even paid-for services can be subject to political decisions, Kovalenko stressed.

The corporation’s materials are used in the airframes and engines of Russian military aircraft.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence has documented the use of the corporation’s titanium products in the manufacture of Su-34 fighter-bombers and Su-35S fighter jets.
Other customers include Aviastar-SP, which manufactures Il-76 military transport aircraft and Il-78 aerial refueling tankers; the Voronezh Joint-Stock Aircraft Manufacturing Company; and the Kamensk-Uralsky Foundry.
In the shipbuilding sector, the Admiralty Shipyards, the Amur Shipbuilding Plant, and the Zvezdochka Ship Repair Center purchase VSMPO-AVISMA products. These enterprises build, repair, and modernize military ships and submarines. In particular, the Admiralty Shipyards builds Project 636.3 diesel-electric submarines equipped with Kalibr-family cruise missiles.
In the armored vehicle sector, the corporation works with Uralvagonzavod, a manufacturer of Russia’s T-72B3 and T-90M tanks. The company purchases metal forgings, stamped components, hatch covers, and other products from VSMPO-AVISMA.

articles.title: Ex-Mossad chief Barnea intended for Iran to see Israel's operations to overwhelm IRGC

When the Mossad took the stunning move of publishing multiple videos in real time of its agents acting against the regime within Iran in June 2025, one of the main reasons was to overwhelm and confuse the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), former Mossad chief David Barnea has revealed.
Leaked on Sunday from comments he made to a closed audience at the Priority Summit this past Thursday.
On June 13, 2025, the Mossad released sensational and rare video footage of its co-lead role with the air force in Israel’s preemptive strike on Iran’s ballistic missiles and air defenses.
Three videos showed the Mossad targeting ballistic missile targets, air defense targets, and general preparations for the attacks (with the agents’ faces covered up).
From the perspective of the videos, it appeared that the Mossad used drones from inside Iran to attack various targets.
Iran had previously accused the Mossad of using drones to attack the Karaj facility in June 2021 as well as other operations.
Mossad's warehouse of drones used to sabotage Iran
It was later confirmed that the Mossad used an entire warehouse of drones to attack and sabotage Iran, along with helping with a large number of remote-controlled vehicles attacking regime targets, and a significant number of human agents on the ground also assisting in assassinations.
Although far more information was quickly publicized about the IDF’s actions, these videos gave readers a rare front-row and real-time seat into what normally were entirely clandestine operations which the Mossad would not even admit to.
Barnea said at the Priority Summit that the video was deliberately published to trigger mass arrests and make it more difficult for the IRGC to identify actual Israeli agents.
“One of the reasons we immediately released an official video on the morning of Operation Rising Lion, with the Mossad logo, was to protect the agents who were there,” Barnea said in a video which Yediot Ahronot shared, and regarding which the Jerusalem Post confirmed the authenticity. “We wanted to make sure they arrested so many people in Iran that they wouldn’t be able to distinguish the wheat from the chaff and would eventually release everyone,” adding that Iran did release all of the detainees.
IRGC arrested over 20,000 people on second day of war
The former Mossad chief said that the IRGC arrested 21,000 people on the second day of the fighting.
“You have to imagine that when you arrest 21,000 people, even if you’ve caught an agent or two, eventually you have to release them because everyone’s story will be the same: I was walking down the street, I was driving a car, they arrested me,” he said, emphasizing that the IRGC would have no way of knowing who was a real agent with such a vast number of detainees,
Barnea added that many of those arrested or executed by the IRGC as “Mossad agents” had nothing to do with the agency.
In addition, he said that nearly all of the Mossad agents were never caught, and at the end of the June 2025 operation, he even publicly taunted the IRGC, issuing a statement, “We will [continue to] be there, like we have been there.”
His explanation may close the book on the unexplained mystery of why the Mossad would have risked broadcasting some of its agents’ actions in real time during the June 2025 operation.
In September 2025, the Post reported exclusively that dozens of Mossad women penetrated Iran and were on the ground performing a variety of kinds of operations during Israel’s attacks on Tehran’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs in June 2025.
While the Mossad does not want to bring too much attention to any one sub-group of potential spies, the Post’s impression was that the Mossad women of 2025 were doing more of every kind of spy role as compared to their sisters of yesterday.
In that same September report, the Post noted that Barnea sent hundreds of Mossad agents, or individuals being run by agents, into operations in Iran simultaneously. All of the varying groups of staff were highly coordinated.
The spy chief directed a project leading to a diverse spectrum of all of the different kinds of agents and backgrounds of those agents one could imagine.
On top of actual Israeli Mossad agents, the spy service has reached new levels in recruiting and training local dissident Iranian agents to act against the ayatollahs’ regime, the Post reported at the time.
While the early 2026 war with Iran is viewed by many as a mixed bag, the June 2025 war was viewed as the most successful Israeli operation of the last three years, along with the exploding beepers used against Hezbollah.

articles.title: Explainer-How Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy sites deepened the rift with Trump
articles.body:
Explainer-How Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy sites deepened the rift with Trump
WASHINGTON, Oct 25 - Relations between US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy took a sharp downward turn in recent weeks, with each leader openly criticizing the other. The two have long had a testy relationship, but Trump's frustration over Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure triggered a crisis that Kyiv's supporters fear could threaten vital US support going forward.
Here's how the relationship soured:
WHAT IS THE HISTORY OF TRUMP-ZELENSKIY TENSIONS?
Trump has been skeptical of US involvement in Ukraine ever since his first term when, shortly after taking office in early 2017, he was asked to provide lethal aid to Ukraine and approved the sale of Javelin missiles to Kyiv.
“Everyone around him wanted him to do it, and they pushed him hard and he eventually signed off on selling them Javelins, very reluctantly,” said a former senior Trump administration official, who spoke on condition of anonymity. “He didn’t consider it a core US interest. It was a European issue.”
Trump's first major encounter with Zelenskiy came in a July 2019 phone call in which the Republican president asked the Ukrainian leader to investigate his Democratic rival Joe Biden and his son Hunter, in exchange for military support Congress had authorized.
That episode led to Trump's first impeachment. Biden beat Trump in the 2020 presidential election.
Trump also has fostered a relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin that runs against the norms of US foreign policy but echoes his warm ties with authoritarian leaders Xi Jinping of China and North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un.
“Trump has always wanted better relations with Russia,” the former official said.
WHAT DEEPENED THE RIFT BETWEEN THE TWO LEADERS?
Trump's current frustration centers on Kyiv's attacks on Russian diesel infrastructure.
Diesel prices have hit record highs since the US and Israel launched a war against Iran in February, and global energy costs spiked. US lawmakers in Trump's Republican party face voter anger over inflation ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
On September 13, Trump began publicly calling on Ukraine to stop targeting diesel infrastructure. The following week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was also concerned that Ukraine had hit US-linked oil shipments.
Ukraine has refused to halt the strikes, saying its long-range drone campaign is its only viable response to nearly five years of Russian bombardment. Moscow was forced in July to ban diesel exports as part of a raft of measures to address domestic fuel shortages.
Angered by Zelenskiy’s defiance, Trump on October 9 announced a deal to buy diesel from Moscow, issuing a temporary general license that allows Russian diesel to reach the global market. He also waived sanctions on Russia authorized by a bill he signed into law in September.
Suriya Jayanti, a former US official who runs a power sector company in Ukraine, said Russia’s strikes on Ukraine’s power grid have increased, despite Trump unilaterally announcing an energy ceasefire on October 11.
"It is clear to everyone in Kyiv that the goal is not actually an energy ceasefire, but it is really just an effort to hobble Ukraine and give Russia a decisive advantage," said Jayanti, who is also a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council think tank.
HAS THE US THREATENED TO CUT OFF SUPPORT TO UKRAINE?
Zelenskiy has said Ukrainian military officials had been threatened by US counterparts, who said continuing the energy strikes would lead the US to cut off intelligence sharing. A US official familiar with the situation disputed Kyiv's account.
Speaking on condition of anonymity, the US official said there has been no increase in pressure on Ukraine.
“We don't have to pressure Zelenskiy. If he wants to make a deal he'll make a deal. I think Putin is putting a ton of pressure on him and he (Zelenskiy) is putting some pressure on Russia but Russia doesn't seem to be minding it as much even though they are getting hit."
On Thursday, Trump said he had asked SpaceX CEO Elon Musk to restore Ukraine’s access to the company's Starlink satellite system. Starlink's disruption temporarily hampered Kyiv's military drone operations and spurred fears that Kyiv would be left defenseless against Russia's attacks going into the winter.
WHAT IS THE STATUS OF MOSCOW-KYIV PEACE TALKS?
Peace efforts have continued but so far have not yielded tangible results.
At talks in Oslo on October 20, Ukraine presented new proposals, and Trump’s son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner repeated Trump's demand that Ukraine stop attacking Russian diesel refineries.
The next day, envoy Witkoff – a close friend of Trump's - met Putin in St. Petersburg. Putin agreed to release detained American Stephen Hubbard in what the two countries called a goodwill gesture.
Zelenskiy said on Friday that negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the US would meet in Abu Dhabi in the first half of November, a possible precursor to a meeting of the three countries’ leaders. The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February. REUTERS

articles.title: Russia hits Ukrainian military logistics hubs – MOD
articles.body:
Russia hits Ukrainian military logistics hubs – MOD
Russian forces have launched an overnight attack targeting the Ukrainian military logistics network in the northeastern Kharkov Region, the Defense Ministry in Moscow has said. The list of targets included three hubs used to store and redistribute supplies for the armed forces and dual-use goods, the ministry said in a statement published on Sunday.
Separately, Russia also struck a bulk freighter in the Black Sea that was carrying military supplies to the Ukrainian port city of Chernomorsk, the ministry added. The attacks were part of a broader operation that involved strikes on Ukrainian energy and transport infrastructure used to support the military, as well as drone storages and launch sites in a total of 159 locations over the past 24 hours.
Ukrainian officials confirmed strikes on the city of Kharkov, adding that an “industrial facility” was among the targets.
Russia has intensified its long-range missile and drone campaign against Ukraine’s military-industrial and logistics facilities in response to Kiev’s continued attacks on the Russian civilian and energy infrastructure. Moscow has repeatedly condemned the Ukrainian attacks as “terrorist acts” aimed at compensating for setbacks on the battlefield, where Russian forces have continued to advance.
According to the Russian Defense Ministry, the nation’s air defense systems intercepted a total of 532 Ukrainian drones during Sunday night alone. The drones were used in attempted attacks on more than two dozen Russian regions, the ministry stated.
Ukraine’s tactics have led to tension between Kiev and Washington. US President Donald Trump stated recently it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president” and find a new person to negotiate peace instead of Vladimir Zelensky, whose presidential term expired more than two years ago. The American president also questioned the Ukrainian leader’s willingness to reach a deal with Moscow and criticized him for continued strikes on Russian oil refineries despite Washington’s repeated requests to stop.
Zelensky has said that Ukraine’s Western backers failed to provide advance warning about Russian ballistic missile launches twice in one week in October. He maintained however, that cooperation between Kiev and Washington had not been suspended, echoing Trump’s earlier remarks in which he said the US is “helping [Ukraine], and we are sharing intel.”
In the meantime, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has accused Kiev of abusing his company’s Starlink civilian satellite internet network to launch offensive drone strikes. According to the US-based businessman, a “loophole” allowing the Ukrainian forces to do so was closed.

articles.title: 'Putin's paranoia' — New air defenses appear around Russian president's Valdai residence, analysis shows
articles.body:
'Putin's paranoia' — New air defenses appear around Russian president's Valdai residence, analysis shows
Russia has built an additional ring of air defense towers within 50 kilometers (30 miles) of Russian President Vladimir Putin's residence in Valdai, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL) and OSINT analyst Jembob reported on Oct. 25.
Valdai is a small town in Russia's northwestern Novgorod Oblast. The town had a population of around 13,600 in 2025, according to Russia's Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat).
The defensive perimeter extends to the Khotilovo military base, which serves as an alternate landing site, and a secret biological laboratory on Lisiy Island, according to RFE/RL.
Satellite images indicate that the new perimeter encompasses both the military airfield in Khotilovo and the laboratory complex on Lisiy Island.
By October, air defense systems believed to be Pantsir or Tor units had been positioned south of Putin's residence, within the 50-kilometer (30-mile) zone.
No positions have yet been identified along the northern section of the perimeter, though additional sites could be established in the coming months, the report said.
One of the towers forming the outer defensive line was already in place by March 2026, on the grounds of the Khotilovo military air base. Putin reportedly uses the base regularly. A dedicated railway branch connects it to his Valdai residence, providing a direct train route, according to RFE/RL.
Other air defense sites have been established along the shores of the Vyshny Volochyok Reservoir.
RFE/RL published an investigation into the secret laboratory on the island on Sept. 3, around the same time construction began on two new air defense towers in the area.
The Kremlin accused Ukraine of attacking Putin's residence in Valdai with more than 90 drones on Dec. 29, 2025. Russian officials claimed the drones were carrying 6-kilogram (13-pound) high-explosive warheads, but claimed that air defenses had allegedly intercepted them all, with no casualties or damage reported.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and the Foreign Ministry denied the allegations, calling them a "lie." Kyiv also accused Moscow of fabricating the claims to undermine Ukraine's standing with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration and derail ongoing peace efforts.
In early January 2026, the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) informed Trump that Ukraine had not targeted Putin's Valdai residence. U.S. intelligence assessed that Ukrainian forces had struck a military facility in the same region that night, but far from the Russian president's residence.

articles.title: America's Wagner Group: Starlink crisis in Ukraine shows dangerous reality for US allies - opinion
articles.body:
On October 14, 2026, Ukraine experienced speed throttling of its connections to Starshield, Starlink’s military counterpart. The imposed strict speed ceilings restricted connections for any terminals or drones exceeding 100 miles per hour.
That grounded or disconnected Ukraine’s faster military strike and interceptor drones, which rely on communication with operators over long distances. Almost as soon as news of the newly imposed limits was disclosed by Ukrainian officials, the game of finger-pointing and shifting the blame between US President Donald Trump and Elon Musk, Starlink’s CEO, began.
Trump announced he had no knowledge of the decision, suggesting the initiative was wholly Musk’s. In turn, Musk claimed to have received orders from the White House. The back-and-forth continued, with both Trump and Musk denying responsibility.
It is not hard to deduce the sequence of events that led to the decision to reduce the coverage: the president and Musk had a conversation, with Trump complaining about Ukraine and how “ungrateful” it was. Musk suggested a way to teach the country a lesson by temporarily reducing Starshield’s services.
The president agreed that it would be a good idea, but suggested the White House should not be directly implicated, given the timing, a few weeks before the midterms, was very sensitive. Yet, no matter how Trump and Musk try to spin the story, the proverbial buck, as put by president Harry Truman, “stops here.”
This avoidance of responsibility is not a new feature of American politics. But the other aspect of the affair has far-reaching consequences, going beyond national borders and carrying worldwide strategic implications.
The US is a superpower possessing one of the most powerful militaries in the world. It is also the major supplier of weapons and military platforms to its allies and countries it deems friendly. Historically, the countries purchasing those weapons understood that their usage and proper maintenance depended on American political goodwill.
The president and Congress could influence or even restrict American-made weapons’ usage and deployment, and many countries have faced those limitations or the threats thereof. Yet it has always been a clear political decision. There was a clear channel of communication to discuss and agree on the matter.
The White House was the responsible party on the American side. Its decisions were politically controlled by internal politics and bilateral relationships. The rules of the game were transparent and well known. That clarity provided the clients of American weaponry a sense of stability and well-placed dependence.
But what if, in the decision to dial down Starshield’s coverage in Ukraine, Musk played a role equal to Trump’s? What if there is a new independent entity in America that can make decisions of a magnitude that, just a few months ago, only the president could?
A slippery slope of who would control Starlink technologies
Elon Musk is not bound by political considerations. His interests are completely independent of those of the president, another country, or bilateral relationships. He is an independent businessman with the power of a sovereign, deciding who wins, who loses, and who dies.
And those decisions are driven not by the art of statecraft, but by his business interests, whims, and caprices. This is not merely the problem of one particular individual, even though, in Musk’s case, that problem is huge.
The wars in Ukraine, Karabakh, and Iran showed how technology has become a decisive force on the battlefield. Those conflicts proved beyond doubt that the huge military conglomerates of yesteryear are no longer capable of providing the technical support a modern military needs to win.
The dinosaurs of old are too slow and cumbersome in a world where a fast pace of development, deployment, and refinement is a must. The American government and the US military have no choice but to rely extensively on start-ups founded by folks with very “interesting” ideas of how the world should be to supply themselves with needed platforms.
Those companies, both private and public, may, as in the case of Starlink, possess dual-use technologies.
Inevitably, the question arises: Who controls the switch? Who controls communication with those devices in the field? The question is of paramount importance because, as Musk has spectacularly displayed, someone in a land far away has the power and ability to stop a war, allow one side to win and another to lose, and effectively play god.
Every American ally in a conflict zone, be it Israel and Ukraine in active wars, Europe awaiting another Russian invasion, Taiwan awaiting China’s channel crossing, or South Korea awaiting another North Korean provocation, is shaken to the core by the Starlink fiasco.
They have all purchased billions of dollars worth of American equipment under the assumption, perhaps no longer true, that its reliability is backed by American political power.
But if that depends on the current state of mind of Musk or another brilliant founder with questionable interests and mental stability, then the US has stopped being an ally, and even a reliable source of weaponry. That means American credibility as a political and military power is lost.
If the American military industry becomes an American version of the Wagner Group, then our power is on a slippery slope to the “dustbin” of history.
The writer lives and works in Silicon Valley, California. He is a founding member of San Francisco Voice for Israel.

articles.title: Russian plant producing Iskander missile components hit in Yelets, 250 km from Ukraine – OSINT
articles.body:
Russian plant producing Iskander missile components hit in Yelets, 250 km from Ukraine – OSINT
The Energiya plant in the Russian city of Yelets in Lipetsk Oblast, which manufactures components for missile systems, was attacked by missiles on the afternoon of 25 October.
Source: analysts from Exilenova+, a Ukrainian OSINT community
Details: Exilenova+ reported that several missiles struck the facility, and smoke was seen across the plant's industrial zone following the hits. Storm Shadow cruise missiles were likely used in the attack on Energiya.
"Everything is burning there at the moment. The area around the strike has been cordoned off, and a large number of ambulances are heading to the plant," the analysts said.
Lipetsk Oblast Governor Igor Artamonov also reported an attack on Yelets. He said a strike had been recorded in the city's industrial zone.
Energiya PJSC specialises in developing and manufacturing electrochemical power sources, including accumulators, power cells and batteries. The facility is of strategic importance because its products are widely used in Russia's military-industrial complex, according to the War&Sanctions project run by Defence Intelligence of Ukraine.
Power cells and batteries manufactured at the Yelets plant are used in the production of Iskander-M cruise missiles, Zircon ballistic missiles, RM-48U missiles, 95Ya6 surface-to-air missiles for Pantsir air defence systems, and Kh-47M2 Kinzhal air-launched ballistic missiles.
Background:
- On 24 October, drones attacked the Omsky Kauchuk chemical plant in Russia, causing a fire at the facility.
- On the same day, Ukraine's defence forces struck the Tolyattikauchuk plant in the Russian city of Tolyatti, Samara Oblast. An explosion and fire were reported following the strike.
