articles.title: Trump rules out Iran strike Sunday as tensions mount across Middle East
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump said Sunday that the United States would not launch an attack on Iran that day, even as tensions between Washington and Tehran continued to simmer, American military forces maintained a heightened presence in the Strait of Hormuz and the State Department ordered some embassy personnel to leave Saudi Arabia.
"There will be no attack on Iran today," Trump told reporters, offering a temporary assurance amid mounting concerns about another round of fighting.
His comments came a day after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu repeated his claim that Iran had resumed its nuclear program. Netanyahu also released a simulation Sunday depicting a nuclear bomb striking Tel Aviv.
Trump, however, disputed the suggestion that Iran was rebuilding its nuclear facilities, saying American intelligence indicated little activity at sites previously bombed by U.S. forces.
Asked in an interview with Fox News whether Iran was attempting to restore damaged nuclear installations and what satellite imagery showed, Trump said Washington had extensive surveillance capabilities.
"We can read the badge on somebody's shirt from space," Trump said. "We know exactly what's going on at Pickaxe Mountain. We know the other three [facilities] are obliterated. They're not moving around there very much."
"We're watching them. We have access to every one of the facilities we bombed. They're covered by thousands of tons of rock," he added.
US commander visits Strait of Hormuz
Meanwhile, Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, visited the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday as American forces continued operations aimed at securing the strategically important waterway.
CENTCOM said Cooper toured the area as U.S. military forces marked what it described as a milestone in helping Gulf partners export more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil since the summer.
During the visit, Cooper flew aboard a CH-47 Chinook helicopter over the international shipping route to assess the operational environment.
According to CENTCOM, more than 3,000 commercial vessels have successfully passed through the strait with American military support over the past six months.
"We continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with our Gulf partners and the shipping industry," Cooper said. "This visit underscores our strong commitment to continued freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz."
The narrow waterway between Iran and Oman connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea and is one of the world's most important maritime routes for oil exports.
CENTCOM said commercial shipping through the strait had gained momentum in recent months after U.S. forces cleared naval mines that it said had been deployed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
The American military said the mine-clearing operations had allowed vessels to resume using the strait's international shipping lanes.
"Today, primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz remain free and clear of Iranian sea mines thanks to incredible efforts by our people," Cooper said.
CENTCOM also claimed that more than 95% of vessels traveling through the strait in recent months had sailed safely despite what it described as unprovoked aggression by the Revolutionary Guard.
The figures, according to the command, demonstrated that the United States and its regional partners maintained control of the international waterway.
US orders embassy staff to leave Saudi Arabia
The State Department confirmed Sunday that it had ordered the departure of nonemergency U.S. government personnel and their family members from the American Embassy in Riyadh amid fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
The confirmation followed reports of diplomatic evacuations from several locations across the Middle East.
"Effective Friday, the Department of State ordered employees to depart Saudi Arabia due to security risks," the department said in a statement.
It cited recent Houthi attacks on Saudi territory, including strikes against civilian airports and other critical infrastructure that had caused civilian casualties and significant travel disruptions.
"The Iran-backed Houthis have carried out acts of aggression against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure," the statement said.
The department warned that the violence could escalate rapidly and spread beyond the areas immediately affected by the fighting.
The evacuation order underscored growing American concerns about the security of diplomatic personnel as hostilities involving Iran and its regional allies threatened to expand.
Sri Lanka evacuates 40 Iranian sailors
In a separate development, Sri Lanka's Foreign Ministry said Sunday that the island nation had coordinated the evacuation of 40 Iranian sailors from 19 commercial vessels operating in international waters near the country.
The operation was conducted at Tehran's request after the sailors experienced unspecified medical problems.
Sri Lankan authorities said Iran had submitted its request through established diplomatic channels and that the sailors had since been returned to the Islamic Republic.
The ministry did not explain why the sailors needed to be evacuated or provide further details about their medical conditions.
Local media outlets, along with India's The Hindu newspaper, reported that the sailors had been aboard oil tankers subject to U.S. sanctions imposed as part of Washington's confrontation with Tehran.
A Sri Lankan government source with direct knowledge of the operation told Reuters that the country's navy and coast guard routinely assist with humanitarian missions.
The latest operation followed Sri Lanka's involvement in rescue and repatriation efforts after a U.S. submarine sank the Iranian warship IRIS Dena with a torpedo off the island's coast on March 4, during the first week of the war involving Israel, the United States and Iran.
Dozens of Iranian sailors were killed in that attack, while Sri Lankan authorities helped rescue survivors.
Sri Lanka subsequently assisted in repatriating the bodies of 87 Iranian sailors, as well as 32 survivors from the Dena and 208 crew members from another Iranian vessel.
Iranians stockpile food and medicine amid fears of renewed war
With Israel's elections two days away and the U.S. midterm elections about a week and a half away, fears of renewed fighting are also growing among ordinary Iranians.
As leaders in Washington, Jerusalem and Tehran exchange warnings and threats, residents of the Iranian capital are preparing for the possibility of another military escalation and further economic disruption.
In interviews with The Associated Press, Tehran residents described stockpiling food, medicine and emergency supplies, while some said they were preparing to leave the city if hostilities resumed.
Fereshteh Hajipour, a 35-year-old mother of a toddler, said she had begun accumulating over-the-counter medications and food in anticipation of a possible war involving more powerful bombs.
The U.S. blockade of Iranian ports has contributed to medicine shortages, according to AP, although there have been no indications of widespread shortages of food or other essential goods.
Iran's economic difficulties have intensified as the rial has fallen to record lows and inflation has surged, severely eroding household purchasing power.
A typical monthly salary in Iran is about 400 million rials, equivalent to roughly $150, leaving many families struggling to afford basic necessities.
"Grocery shopping can cost half a month's salary," said Mohammad Mohammadi, 36.
Despite soaring prices, some residents said they felt compelled to purchase additional supplies because of the confrontation in the Strait of Hormuz and the possibility that trade disruptions could worsen.
Mohammad Abdi, 39, said he had stocked up on dried dates, cooking oil and rice for his family.
"I'm worried the situation could get worse," he said.
Others are preparing to leave Tehran altogether.
Hashem Vajdani, a 45-year-old fitness trainer, said he had already packed his belongings and planned to seek refuge in a smaller town in northern Iran if fighting resumed.
"I've already packed my things to go to a safer town in the north of the country," he said. "Today I bought more canned food, crackers and extra blankets."

articles.title: Zelensky details expectations for upcoming trilateral peace talks with Russia, US
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky outlined his expectations for upcoming trilateral peace negotiations, and discussed air defenses and the planned ceasefire in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in an interview on Oct. 25.
In an exclusive interview with Alla Mazur, host of "TSN The Week," Zelensky detailed Ukraine's readiness to meet with Russian and American teams for peace negotiations scheduled for early November.
Above all, Zelensky stressed the need for robust security guarantees for Ukraine in any deal aimed at ending the war.
"Our security guarantees are our guarantees, and they cannot be dictated by the Russian side," Zelensky said. "Restrictions on our army and Ukraine's neutrality are not up for discussion."
The question of NATO's involvement in Ukrainian security will "undoubtedly" come up in the negotiations, Zelensky said. The president suggested that if Ukraine is not allowed to join NATO, European countries and the U.S. should agree to extend the body's Article 5 defensive pact to Ukraine. Ukraine would also need to maintain a strong army after a peace deal is reached. 
"The best, in my opinion, is NATO plus a strong Ukrainian army, as part of the alliance," Zelensky said. "If I have enough finances, I want to keep the army of 800,000 people. We decide for ourselves what our army will be. If we are in NATO, the number can be 800,000 or less. But it will be a question of who is willing to finance or co-finance with us."
Before a meeting between Zelensky, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and U.S. President Donald Trump can take place, technical talks among the three countries' negotiating teams must be held first, said Zelensky.
"The issue of territory is a red line that can only be discussed at the level of leaders," Zelensky said. "Everyone should understand: first, we are not exchanging anything for anything. We are ready to discuss. If it's a territorial issue, then at the level of leaders. Other issues can be discussed at the level of technical groups."
As part of the negotiations, Zelensky said he was prepared to discuss an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, establishing a new deal to protect grain shipments in the Black Sea, and prisoner exchanges.
"Energy, grain, and people – these are the specifics," Zelensky said. "A meeting at the level of leaders is an opportunity to achieve those specifics after our trilateral meeting. That's what we are asking for and offering."
Zelensky said that by offering these points for negotiation, a refusal by the Russian team to engage on the items will help expose whether the Kremlin is serious about peace with Ukraine or not.
"We are not demanding, but rather offering this to the American side," Zelensky said. "That would demonstrate seriousness. But if it's just a political maneuver and Putin is simply saying, 'Yes, I'm ready,' because he doesn't want to escalate tensions with America before the [midterm] elections, we will very quickly see in November whether it was a trick or not."
The president also warned that loosening sanctions on Russia before the negotiations would weaken Ukraine's leverage. This follows Trump waiving sanctions on Russian oil exports in October in an attempt to ease oil prices heightened by his war with Iran.
"I don't want us to be left without tools – without sanctions, without money, or without frozen assets – at the meeting with Putin," Zelensky said. "Because then, as Mr. Trump said, we will really have very few cards in our hand."
Turning his attention to the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, Zelensky said that the planned Oct. 27 ceasefire would need to last several days and include Russian assistance.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Residents face severe shortages of food, water, and electricity, while mined roads and constant drone attacks make safe evacuation virtually impossible.
"Of course, Russia will do everything it can to clear the roads in a way that encourages people to go towards Russia and stay there; they won't simply let people go," Zelensky said. "Some people will be evacuated to Ukraine – to the part that we control – in one format or another. The most important thing is to unblock the people so they can live. Ideally, they should be able to reach their destination and evacuate here, to us, to Ukraine, where they will receive everything they need and be supported."
Zelensky also detailed his conversations with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo, Norway, in October that set the stage for the planned round of trilateral negotiations. In meeting with Witkoff, Zelensky said they discussed limits placed on Ukraine's Starlink military systems, restrictions on intelligence the U.S. shares with Kyiv, and air defense shortages.
While the issues plaguing Ukrainian forces' use of Starlink systems and the matter of American intelligence sharing have been resolved for now, Zelensky stressed that Kyiv still lacked key air defense assistance.
"There is progress; it's just very slow," Zelensky said. "It's not enough to simply say, 'Yes, we will give [Patriot missiles] to you,' and then not deliver them for a month or two. That simply doesn't work."

articles.title: Saudi says Riyadh airport partly reopens despite renewed Houthi threats but little traffic
articles.body:
Saudi says Riyadh airport partly reopens despite renewed Houthi threats
- Saudi Arabia partly reopened Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport after an Oct 10 Houthi attack killed 13 people, but flight traffic stayed very low.
- The Houthis said the airport was still a “military target” and warned it would “never be safe”, as missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia continued.
- The wider Yemen war is worsening regional tensions, shattering the UN truce and putting Saudi Arabia under pressure near key Red Sea and Gulf shipping routes.
AI generated
Saudi Arabia said its main airport resumed operations at two terminals on Oct 25 even as Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis vowed to keep striking the facility, which they called a “military target”.
King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh had halted operations on Oct 10 following an attack claimed by the Houthis that killed 13 people, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.
Saudi Arabia said it intercepted another wave of missiles and drones on Oct 25 as fighting with the militant group continued unabated.
The Houthis said they had launched attacks on the air hub among other sites in the kingdom, including in Khamis Mushait and Jazan. It was not immediately clear if those were the strikes the kingdom said it had blocked.
The conflict has become an increasingly destabilising element in the US-Israeli offensive against Iran, turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war.
Flight tracking data shows little traffic
After the Saudi authorities announced the partial resumption of operations at the airport, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree vowed the facility would “never be safe” and urged airlines, airport staff and travellers not to use it.
Late on Oct 24, the airport said Terminal 1 would be designated for domestic flights and Terminal 2 for international flights operated by national carriers starting Oct 25.
Despite the announcement, flight tracking data from Flightradar24 showed little traffic at the airport on Oct 25.
The Saudi-led coalition said earlier in October that the Houthis had carried out 20 attacks on the airport between Oct 1 and 11.
Missile and drone attacks continue
Saudi civil defence said on Oct 25 that shrapnel from the interception of two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis over Khamis Mushait and Ahad Rafidah injured two people and damaged residential buildings and vehicles.
The civil defence authorities earlier issued emergency alerts for Riyadh and the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran on Oct 25, before saying minutes later that the danger had passed.
The coalition said two drones and a ballistic missile were launched towards Riyadh, and a cruise missile towards the southern city of Khamis Mushait. It later said it intercepted 10 ballistic missiles fired towards southern Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis said they attacked the airport and Saudi oil facilities on Oct 24. The Saudi authorities did not comment directly on the Houthi statements.
Saudi Arabia has stepped up its strikes against the Houthis after the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month, closing in on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait – a global maritime chokepoint and shipping route for Gulf oil producers on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula to the Strait of Hormuz.
The renewed fighting in Yemen has shattered a UN-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022.
Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen’s civil war in 2015 at the head of a coalition supporting the internationally recognised government, after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa a year earlier. REUTERS

articles.title: US midterms could restore Ukraine’s American aid and curb Trump’s Russia deals, if Democrats win Congress
articles.body:
If Democrats win the House, and possibly the Senate, a result nonpartisan analysts call plausible, they would gain the power to bring new Ukraine aid to a vote and to push back on President Donald Trump’s deals easing pressure on Russia, Reuters reports in an analysis of how US foreign policy could shift.
The stakes are concrete. Trump has largely halted direct US aid to Ukraine, which lawmakers of both parties had backed, and its current supplies run from packages passed under his predecessor.
Weeks ago, he also waived the sanctions on Russian energy that Congress had written into law and struck a deal to bring Russian diesel back to the market, angering Republicans and Democrats alike.
What a Democratic Congress could do for Ukraine
With both chambers, Democrats could put new Ukraine aid on the floor, and given the bipartisan support such aid has drawn, it could pass with the two-thirds majorities needed to override a Trump veto.
Other steps could be taken, too. Representative Gregory Meeks of New York, in line to chair the House Foreign Affairs Committee if his party wins control, has already introduced bipartisan legislation to block Trump’s plan to return Russian diesel to the global market.
Democrats are also readier than Trump’s Republicans to rein in military spending. They blocked his request for an unprecedented 67% rise in the military budget, to $1.5 trillion, in the Senate, and many say they will try to restore the foreign aid he has withheld or canceled.
The limits of a slice of power
The leverage has limits. Even with both chambers, Democrats would still face a president who can veto, and overriding him would require two-thirds of each chamber. The pattern has already been visible in Iran: Trump launched that war on 28 February without congressional approval, and when a War Powers resolution passed with a handful of Republican votes, his administration ignored it.

articles.title: Israeli opposition leaders accuse Netanyahu of spreading ‘terror, panic’ ahead of election
articles.body:
Zein Khalil and Rania Abushamala
25 October 2026•Update: 25 October 2026
Two Israeli opposition leaders accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday of spreading “terror” and “panic” among Israelis ahead of the country’s parliamentary election.
Netanyahu posted an artificial intelligence-generated image early Sunday depicting a nuclear explosion in Tel Aviv, accompanied by a warning about the threat of Iran acquiring nuclear weapons and a call to continue confronting Tehran during the remainder of US President Donald Trump’s term.
Gadi Eisenkot, a former Israeli army chief and leader of the Yashar party, accused Netanyahu of hysteria and resorting to the same tactics he used in previous election campaigns: “lies and spreading fear.”
“This time, you are threatening Israeli citizens with total destruction, after failing to achieve the goals of the war in Iran,” Eisenkot wrote on the US social media platform X.
He added that Netanyahu had shifted from promising “absolute victory” to the slogan “We will not surrender.”
“That is the whole story,” he said.
Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats party, also criticized Netanyahu in a post on X.
“The prime minister of Israel posted a picture of an atomic bomb over Tel Aviv,” Golan wrote.
He called for the Israeli premier to be barred from social media, saying Netanyahu and those around him had “lost their minds” as pressure mounted.
“On Tuesday, we will replace those spreading panic and restore security and rationality to Israel,” Golan added.
The exchanges came two days before Israel’s parliamentary election, scheduled for Oct. 27, amid a tight competition between Netanyahu’s political camp and opposition parties seeking to end his rule.
Netanyahu has focused much of his recent campaign on security threats, particularly Iran’s nuclear program, while opposition figures have accused him of exploiting those concerns for political gains.
On Wednesday, Eisenkot said Netanyahu’s claim that he had destroyed Iranian nuclear bombs and saved Israel was “an outright lie,” adding that “Iran has never possessed nuclear bombs.”
In an interview with Israel’s public broadcaster KAN, Eisenkot also said he did not see an immediate and direct threat that would justify launching a military attack on Iran ahead of the election.
Netanyahu has led a far-right government since late 2022, widely described as the most right-wing in Israel’s history.

articles.title: Houthis fire missiles at Saudi Arabia as Riyadh airport reopens
articles.body:

Houthis fire missiles at Saudi Arabia as Riyadh airport reopens
Yemen's Houthis launched wide-ranging strikes across swathes of southern Saudi Arabia on Sunday, as the kingdom announced the partial reopening of Riyadh's international airport despite repeated attacks by the group.
Alerts warning of possible attacks were activated across the kingdom's south throughout the day, with the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis saying at least 10 ballistic missiles were intercepted.
Saudi Arabia, which leads a military coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis, has faced a barrage of strikes from the group in recent weeks.
The fighting erupted after a years-long truce between the Houthis and Yemen's Riyadh-backed government fell apart.
"The bombardment has been very heavy since this morning - may God keep us safe. Everything is shaking because of the explosions," one resident in Khamis Mushait told AFP Sunday on condition of anonymity.
Further north, Riyadh's international airport said flights would resume on Sunday after a two-week closure following the Houthi strikes.
However it remained unclear to what extent the airport was operational.
The Houthi fighters have carried out waves of strikes on the airport, including an attack this month that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.
The group has also targeted oil infrastructure and other sites.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned that Riyadh airport was still "unsafe" and a "military target".
"The Yemeni Armed Forces warn all international, regional and local airlines - as well as staff and travellers - against using King Khalid Airport in Riyadh, as it is unsafe and serves as a military target for our forces," he said.
"The Saudi regime shall bear the consequences of any operations at the airport."
Attack warning
As the airport prepared to open, AFP journalists in Riyadh heard three explosions in the early hours of Sunday, with residents receiving alert messages for a "hostile aerial threat" urging them to stay in a safe place.
The warning came as the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had downed a ballistic missile launched by the group towards the capital, as well as two drones in the capital area.
"Air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh," the coalition posted on X.
Later Sunday morning, the coalition said its forces intercepted a cruise missile fired by the Houthis at the kingdom's southern city of Khamis Mushait.
Attacks appeared to target areas across the south, with warnings also issued for Abha city along with areas in Taif, Namas and Jazan.
The attacks came after the Houthi fighters said that - in the space of 24 hours - they targeted three Saudi airports, including in Riyadh, energy installations, a pipeline and an air base.
The Saudi civil defence agency said it had also responded to falling debris in the Mecca and Medina regions on Saturday after intercepting two Houthi missiles.
The Houthis denied targeting the cities, the two holiest in Islam, calling the Saudi claim a "huge lie".
The Houthis also fired at the southern Yemeni city of Aden, the interim seat of the Saudi-backed government, saying they targeted a naval base and military camp overseen by Saudi forces.
The flare-up in Yemen, with the Houthis taking control of the entire Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive last month, has further destabilised the region and disrupted oil markets.
The Houthi attacks have dealt a blow to Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest exporter of crude, disrupting businesses, airlines and residents, and rattling its drive to shift its international image.

articles.title: Ukraine-US-Russia Talks May Resume in November as Trump Eyes Business With Both Sides
articles.body:
The Kremlin is prepared to resume trilateral negotiations with Ukraine and the United States after November 4, Russian President Vladimir Putin’s foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov told state-controlled outlet Vesti on October 25, as U.S. President Donald Trump said Washington could do business with both Moscow and Kyiv after the war ends.
Ushakov’s remarks followed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s statement on October 23 that another round of trilateral talks was expected in the first half of November, with Abu Dhabi among the possible venues.
“The next deadline is now Nov. 4, our major holiday. After that, we will be ready to resume negotiations,” Ushakov said, referring to Russia’s National Unity Day.
The Kremlin has repeatedly dismissed ceasefire proposals, insisting that Kyiv surrender the parts of the Donbas region in eastern Ukraine that Russian forces have not captured. The territory is strategically important, and handing it over would give Moscow land its military has been unable to take on the battlefield. Ukraine, meanwhile, has accepted several ceasefire proposals put forward by Washington.
Ushakov said he did not anticipate major progress at the first trilateral meeting after the pause, describing it as a “trial run.” He added that a peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine “still needs work.”
On October 20, U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Zelensky and European partners, including Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store.
Witkoff met Putin in St. Petersburg the following day for three hours. Afterward, the Kremlin said it was prepared to restart trilateral negotiations in November. Witkoff said on October 21 that discussions involving Ukrainian, American and Russian representatives would “continue at the technical level.”
Putin has long avoided direct talks with Zelensky. Instead, the Russian leader is reportedly seeking a meeting with Trump in China next month in an effort to secure a favorable peace agreement without Ukraine’s participation.
In recent weeks, Trump has criticized Zelensky, announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine without agreement from both sides that ultimately failed, threatened to halt intelligence-sharing with Kyiv and eased restrictions on Russian oil exports. Trump has defended the sanctions relief, arguing that it could encourage Moscow to negotiate with Ukraine.
Trump said on October 24 that he expected the United States to resume commercial dealings with both countries once the war was over, despite criticism of efforts to restore business ties with Russia.
The remarks came as the first tanker carrying Russian diesel under a supply agreement announced by Trump on October 9 was heading from the Baltic port of Primorsk to New York. The vessel is due to deliver 40,000 metric tons of fuel.
Following the announcement of the deal, Moscow partially relaxed restrictions on diesel exports, allowing 500,000 metric tons to be sold.
“Certainly, we'll do business with Ukraine and with Russia after this war ends, I would think,” Trump said. He added that he wanted to “get back to life where Russia and Ukraine make a deal, and then we'd be able to do business with both.”
The U.S. president also argued that Washington should have obtained greater financial compensation for the billions of dollars in assistance provided to Kyiv during Joe Biden’s presidency.
“I feel foolish because all you had to do is ask them, and they would have paid. Meaning the EU would have paid,” Trump said.
Plans to import about 900,000 metric tons of Russian diesel over the coming months have drawn criticism from European allies, Ukraine and members of Congress. Critics say the shipments would circumvent sanctions imposed on Moscow over its war against Ukraine.
The delivery would be the first shipment of Russian diesel to the United States since 2022, when then-President Joe Biden prohibited imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in response to the invasion of Ukraine.
The agreement comes as tensions between Washington and Kyiv deepen, with Ukraine facing restrictions on Starlink access and reported delays in deliveries of Patriot air defense interceptors.
Trump has intensified his attacks on Zelensky, accusing the Ukrainian president of refusing to end the war and calling for him to be replaced.
The resumption of Russian diesel imports also comes as Republicans face a difficult political environment ahead of the November 3 U.S. midterm elections, with recent polling showing declining support for Trump.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll published on October 19 found that only 31% of Americans approved of Trump’s performance, the lowest rating of either of his presidential terms. Meanwhile, 47% of registered voters said they would support Democrats if congressional elections were held that day, compared with 35% who favored Republicans, giving Democrats a 12-point lead, their largest of the current election cycle.

articles.title: NSM Missile System Evolves with Container-Based Launcher
articles.body:
Norwegian company KONGSBERG has successfully conducted launch tests of its Naval Strike Missile (NSM) anti-ship missile from a standard 20-foot shipping container. The new system is called the NSM Mission Module.
KONGSBERG announced the development in a press release.
The tests took place in Norway. The missile was launched from a container-based launch system that can accommodate up to four missiles. The tests were designed to verify safety, transportation and loading logistics, and the system’s ability to withstand pressure and blast effects during launch.
According to the company, the containerized solution offers an alternative approach to deploying missile systems. Integrating the launcher into a standard shipping container simplifies transportation, relocation between positions, and the use of existing logistics and transport networks.
https://t.co/GA1WuaKAh3
— dimdim (@dimdim518484) October 24, 2026
The container-based launch system can be deployed from ships, trucks, or directly from the ground without modifications. This allows greater operational flexibility, particularly in regions with extensive coastlines and long distances.
“A containerized solution can be pre-positioned and deployed discreetly to support operations wherever the need arises. Meanwhile, it enables capabilities to be distributed across larger areas, providing greater operational flexibility and more deployment options,” Ståle Mortensson, Vice President BD & Strategy in Missiles & Aerostructures at KONGSBERG, shared.
The Naval Strike Missile (NSM) is a subsonic, precision-guided cruise missile designed to engage both surface and land targets. The missile is powered by a TRI-40 turbojet engine for cruise flight, combined with a solid-propellant rocket booster for launch.
Norwegian company KONGSBERG developed the missile. It is about 4 m long and weighs around 410 kg at launch. The NSM carries a 120 kg combined-effects warhead. Its stated range is over 185 km.
During the midcourse phase of flight, the missile is guided by an inertial navigation system (INS), with GPS signals providing corrections.
During the terminal phase of flight, the missile uses an imaging infrared (IIR) seeker combined with an automatic target recognition system that relies on an onboard database of target thermal signatures. This enables the missile to identify specific target types and select the intended target.
In early July 2026, Ukraine reported having a mobile coastal defense system armed with NSM anti-ship missiles in service.
The Office of the President of Ukraine published a photograph of its launcher during Volodymyr Zelensky’s working visit to the Odesa region. Its delivery had not been publicly reported before then.

articles.title: Netanyahu posts image of atomic bomb over Tel Aviv: ‘Nothing else will matter’
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday shared an AI-generated image depicting an atomic bomb falling on Tel Aviv, accompanied by a stark warning about Iran's nuclear ambitions, just two days before Israelis head to the polls. The post, which suggested that domestic political controversies pale in comparison with the threat from Tehran, drew a sharp response from Democrats party chairman Yair Golan, who accused Netanyahu of spreading panic.
Alongside the image, Netanyahu quoted Yuval Bloomberg, an Israeli writer and political commentator best known for his book The Oslo Trap, which critically examines the 1993 Oslo Accords and their consequences for Israeli security.
"The State of Israel faces a real and tangible existential threat," Bloomberg wrote. "If the Iranians obtain nuclear weapons, nothing else will matter anymore. Everything is so trivial compared with the existential danger posed by Iran and the Shiite axis."
The post also repeated the argument that Israel has only two more years under U.S. President Donald Trump's administration to address the Iranian threat, portraying disputes dominating Israeli politics as distractions from the country's most pressing security challenge.
"Qatar, the ultra-Orthodox, Urich, military conscription, warnings. It's all one giant smokescreen designed to conceal the one issue that towers above everything else," the post read. "If two atomic bombs fall on central Israel, who will care about all these meaningless controversies?"
The image and accompanying message came as Israel entered the final stretch of its election campaign, with voters set to cast their ballots Tuesday, October 27. Netanyahu has emphasized the threat from Iran throughout the campaign, arguing that confronting Tehran's nuclear ambitions must remain Israel's overriding national priority.
Golan, a former IDF deputy chief of staff and chairman of the Democrats party, condemned the post and accused the prime minister of attempting to frighten voters.
"The prime minister of Israel has posted an image of an atomic bomb falling on Tel Aviv," Golan said. "I ask that he be kept away from social media. The man and those around him have lost it. The pressure is mounting."
Golan also linked his criticism directly to the upcoming election, saying: "On Tuesday, we will replace those spreading panic and restore security and sanity to Israel."

articles.title: Houthis renew strikes on Saudi airports and oil facilities
articles.body:
Houthis renew strikes on Saudi airports and oil facilities
Yemen’s Houthis have struck several targets in Saudi Arabia, including two international airports and energy infrastructure facilities operated by the oil giant Saudi Aramco, the group’s military spokesman said on Saturday.
The conflict between Yemen’s Ansar Allah movement, also known as the Houthis, and the Saudi-led coalition escalated last month, when the militant group seized the Red Sea port cities of Mocha and Dhubab as well as Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Houthis have since tightened their siege of Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city and a key stronghold of anti-Houthi forces.
In a statement posted on X, Yahya Saree said the Houthis had conducted seven operations using ballistic missiles and drones, targeting King Khalid Airport in Riyadh, King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, Najran Airport and Khamis Mushait Air Base, as well as Aramco’s facilities in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery and crude oil pumping stations, and a pipeline linking eastern and western Saudi Arabia.
The spokesman said the attacks were carried out in response to what the group described as Saudi “aggression” against Yemen. Saree claimed Saudi forces had launched 100 airstrikes over the previous 24 hours, targeting civilian infrastructure in Sanaa and other areas, leaving dozens dead and wounded. 
He said the Houthis would continue attacking Saudi territory until the “aggression” ends and the Saudi-led coalition lifts its restrictions on the movement of goods and people into and out of Yemen.
The latest attack came as Riyadh’s main air hub prepared to resume operations after more than two weeks of disruption following earlier Houthi strikes. The facility announced a partial reopening from Sunday. In a separate post on X, Saree warned that airlines, airport staff and passengers against using the site, calling it a military target and saying it would remain unsafe.
The spokesman also accused Riyadh of spreading false claims that the Houthis had targeted the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, insisting that the group’s operations were directed solely at Saudi oil facilities and military bases and were announced as they took place.
The accusation came in response to Saudi Civil Defense claims that debris from the interception of two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis fell in the Mecca and Medina regions on Saturday. The debris landed in several locations, including Wadi Al-Mughammas in Mecca, Jeddah, Taif and Rabigh, the agency said on Saturday.
Yemen’s civil war began in 2014, with Saudi Arabia leading a military intervention the following year to support the internationally recognized government against the Houthis. Fighting eased under a UN-brokered truce in 2022 but escalated sharply in September 2026.
The renewed conflict has seen the Houthis launch missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities, while the Riyadh-led coalition has intensified airstrikes on Houthi positions, command centers and weapons networks.
The Houthis have claimed the total number of Saudi airstrikes and missile attacks since the latest escalation began has reached 3,123.

articles.title: Russian titanium plant in Urals reportedly hit by Ukrainian drones, 1,500 km from Ukraine

The reported strike highlights Ukraine’s ability to reach industrial facilities deep inside Russia that support its military-industrial complex.
AVISMA produces titanium materials used in aviation and aerospace manufacturing, including military aircraft, aircraft engines, missiles, and space technology, according to Exilenova+.
Regional governor Dmitry Makhonin said the industrial facility sustained damage but continued operating normally. He said five workers were injured in the attack.
A target deep inside Russia
Perm Krai lies in Russia’s Ural region, roughly 1,500 km from Ukraine’s border. The distance places the reported strike far beyond Russia’s border regions, where Ukrainian drone attacks have frequently targeted military and industrial infrastructure.
The reported attack follows a broader Ukrainian campaign against Russian industrial and energy facilities linked to the country’s war effort.
Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed that air defenses intercepted and destroyed 532 Ukrainian drones overnight across 23 Russian regions and over the Sea of Azov, according to Russian state news agency TASS.
The reported interceptions included drones over Perm Krai, as well as regions around Moscow and areas in southern and western Russia. The figures have not been independently verified.
The extent of damage at AVISMA and any impact on its operations have not been independently established.

Late on Saturday, the airport said Terminal 1 would be designated for domestic flights and Terminal 2 for international flights operated by national carriers starting Sunday.
Despite the announcement, flight tracking data from Flightradar24 showed little traffic at the airport on Sunday.
The airport had halted operations on October 10 following an attack claimed by the Houthis that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.
The Saudi-led coalition said earlier this month that the Houthis had carried out 20 attacks on King Khalid International Airport between October 1 and 11.
Missile, drone attacks continue
Saudi civil defense authorities issued emergency alerts for Riyadh and the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran on Sunday, before saying minutes later that the danger had passed.
The coalition said two drones and a ballistic missile were launched towards Riyadh, and a cruise missile towards the southern city of Khamis Mushait. It later said it intercepted 10 ballistic missiles fired towards southern Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis said they attacked the airport and Saudi oil facilities on Saturday. Saudi authorities did not comment directly on the Houthi statements.
Saudi Arabia has stepped up its strikes against the Houthis after the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month, closing in on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait – a global maritime chokepoint and shipping route for Gulf oil producers on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula to the Strait of Hormuz.
The renewed fighting in Yemen has shattered a UN-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022. Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war in 2015 at the head of a coalition supporting the internationally recognized government, after the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, a year earlier.

articles.title: Trump uses Michigan rally to attack Democratic Senate candidate El-Sayed
articles.body:
Yasin Gungor
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
US President Donald Trump used a campaign rally Sunday to launch fierce attacks against Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed while endorsing his Republican rival Mike Rogers ahead of the November midterm elections.
"I'm here today in Michigan for a very important reason. I'm here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator, and that's the fact. Not going to let that happen," he told the crowd during his 26th rally in 12 days.
Trump claimed that El-Sayed would require a metal detector to enter the chamber, accusing him of wanting to abolish police and federal border enforcement agencies.
The Michigan race pits El-Sayed against Rogers to fill the vacancy left by retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, representing a critical battleground for party control in the Senate.
Urging supporters to turn out on Nov. 3, Trump warned that voter participation drops when his name is absent from the ballot.
"Please show up and vote, because essentially we are all on the ballot," he said.
He also targeted Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar, alleging that she used an alternate name to assume office and demanding her immediate resignation from Congress while disparaging Somalia. The remarks follow heightened political friction after federal agents executed an early-morning search warrant at Omar's Washington, DC residence on Oct. 12.
Addressing international matters, Trump attributed urban unrest in France, Italy and Spain entirely to immigration.
"I didn't see any students there. These were a lot of large men with very big muscles," he said, recalling how he cautioned French President Emmanuel Macron in 2017 about border policies.
European cities have recently witnessed street demonstrations linked to economic pressures and migration debates.
Trump also voiced frustration toward Norway over the Nobel Peace Prize, arguing that he resolved eight conflicts without receiving recognition after the Nobel Committee awarded the 2025 prize to Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado.
"I don't want anybody from Norway," he said, contrasting it with Denmark, which he said was "great,” praising them for cooperating on a security and defense framework regarding Greenland.
Speaking to reporters prior to the rally, Trump said Washington is "getting close to a deal" with Canada, alleging that Ottawa has long profited off the US. Bilateral trade remains strained after both countries imposed tariffs on billions of dollars of goods following the collapse of trade negotiations.
Asked about subterranean uranium in Iran, he dismissed immediate proliferation risks, citing heavy rock coverage at targeted facilities alongside continuous surveillance by the US Space Force.
Strains persist across the Middle East as the Iran war remains unresolved following large-scale American and Israeli military strikes on Iran.
Trump also claimed the US defeated Iran “militarily, financially and otherwise” and said the war will end “quite soon, one way or the other.”

articles.title: U.S. Considers Using Bombers in Air Combat
articles.body:
The U.S. Air Force is considering deploying bombers in air-to-air combat to strengthen its fighter force.
The War Zone reports the development, citing a U.S.Air Force report to Congress.
The approach is being considered as part of planning for the future composition of the aircraft fleet and exploring additional capabilities to counter China’s air forces.
The U.S. Air Force plans to have 1,509 combat aircraft in its operational fleet by 2035. At the same time, the service estimates its total requirement at 1,723 aircraft.
Achieving the planned fleet size will depend on stable funding, the rate at which new aircraft are produced, and the industry’s ability to deliver the required numbers.
One option being considered is using the next-generation B-21 Raider stealth bomber in air combat. Its long range, stealth capabilities, large payload capacity, and advanced sensors could allow it to perform not only ground-strike missions but also air-to-air combat roles.
The bombers could carry long-range air-to-air missiles or a large number of smaller missiles.
In this role, bombers could engage aerial targets at long distances while operating alongside fighter jets and other platforms. However, the U.S. military noted in the report that it is evaluating several options to expand its air combat capabilities.
These include buying additional fighter jets and using Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) drones more often.
The U.S. military has not yet specified which bombers could receive these capabilities, what weapons they would carry, or when work on the initiative might begin.
In recent years, the Pentagon has been actively developing capabilities to counter Chinese air power. This is reflected in the weapons being introduced into U.S. military aviation, including the AIM-260, AIM-174, and AIM-424 Malice missiles, as well as the prospective Air Force Long Range Weapon – a missile with a range of at least 1,850km.
Militarnyi previously reported that the U.S. Air Force was preparing to hold a closed-door meeting with defense contractors to outline requirements for a new very-long-range air-to-air missile.

articles.title: Lithuania Develops X-12 Jet-Powered Interceptor Drone, Already Tested in Ukraine
articles.body:
Lithuania has presented the X-12, a jet-powered interceptor drone designed to destroy fast-moving aerial targets, including Russia’s Geran-5 drones.
According to the Lithuanian news outlet Delfi, the drone has already been tested in combat in Ukraine.
Representatives of the Strategic Defense Alliance (SDA), an association of Ukrainian, Lithuanian, and Latvian defense technology companies, shared that the X-12 is expected to be supplied to the Ukrainian military.
The X-12 is powered by a turbojet engine and, according to its developers, can reach a maximum speed of up to 700km/h. Its cruising speed is approximately 350 km/h.
The drone has a reported range of up to 126 km and a maximum operating altitude of 10 km. Depending on its configuration and payload, its flight endurance can exceed 12 minutes.
According to Richardas Savickas, a representative of the Strategic Defense Alliance (SDA), the developers aimed to make the X-12 interceptor less expensive than its target, such as a Shahed drone, and eliminate the use of Chinese components.
He claims that the drone contains no Chinese-made parts: its engines were assembled in Lithuania, while some of its other components were manufactured in Latvia and Ukraine.
Cooperation with Ukraine involves not only participation in development and joint manufacturing, but also testing under combat conditions. Savickas emphasized that such technologies could not be tested without Ukrainian partners, as Lithuania lacks the necessary conditions.
According to Savickas, Ukrainian military personnel who tested the X-12 gave its capabilities a positive assessment. He added that the drone is also planned for delivery to Ukraine.
“Ukrainian military personnel who have tested this technology are very satisfied. At present, the X-12 has no equivalent. It is a truly exceptional technology. In general, we anticipated that Russia would switch to jet engines. We have been practically keeping pace with these developments,” he said.
Lithuania is also considering integrating the X-12 into its own air defense system. Tadas Ruzhele, coordinator of Lithuanian-Ukrainian defense industry cooperation at Lithuania’s Ministry of National Defence, described such technologies as a critically important component of a layered air defense system. However, he stressed that effective protection requires a combination of different capabilities, trained operators, and the incorporation of lessons learned from Ukraine’s combat experience.
Ukraine had previously developed a jet-powered interceptor based on the Bars missile-drone, which is planned for joint production with Germany.

articles.title: France Deploys Maritime Patrol Aircraft to Protect Black Sea Shipping
articles.body:
France has deployed an Atlantique 2 maritime patrol aircraft for operations in the Black Sea following a series of drone attacks on merchant vessels near the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria.
The Romanian media outlet Curs de Guvernare reported this, citing flight-tracking data for military aircraft.
According to the publication, a French Navy Atlantique 2 (ATL2) maritime patrol aircraft arrived in Constanța, Romania, on October 18.
On October 24, France’s Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said during a visit to Varna, Bulgaria, that the Atlantique 2 had been operating in the region for two weeks as part of NATO missions.
According to the minister, the French aircraft had also taken part in rescue operations following recent attacks on merchant vessels. Barrot recalled that three vessels had been attacked, one of which sank within minutes about 100 kilometers from Varna.
Meanwhile, a U.S. Navy Boeing P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol and anti-submarine warfare aircraft, which arrived from Naval Air Station Sigonella in Sicily, patrolled the western Black Sea near the Bulgarian coast.
Militarnyi previously reported on the deployment of a U.S. P-8A Poseidon to patrol Bulgarian waters on October 19.
The deployment of additional patrol aircraft comes amid a deteriorating security situation in the western Black Sea.
On October 17, two Romanian Air Force F-16 fighters shot down two Geran-family strike drones that had violated Romanian airspace over the country’s territorial waters.
Following the series of attacks, Romania initiated a meeting of the North Atlantic Council, which took place in Brussels on October 20.
Following the meeting, NATO decided to strengthen surveillance of the Black Sea, including through additional patrol aircraft, radar systems, drones and reconnaissance units.

articles.title: Zelensky undermines Trump more than Iran and Cuba do – Medvedev
articles.body:
Zelensky undermines Trump more than Iran and Cuba do – Medvedev
Vladimir Zelensky’s disregard for Donald Trump is doing more damage to the US president’s interests than Iran, Cuba, and Venezuela do combined, former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev said on Sunday.
Ukraine’s leader has publicly backed Trump’s predecessor and former political rival, Joe Biden, rejected US proposals to settle the Ukraine conflict and worked to turn European leaders against Trump, Medvedev alleged.
“The Kiev scumbag regularly spits straight in the face of the US president, ignoring his demands and turning influential Americans (and not-so-influential Europeans) against him,” Medvedev, who currently serves as deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, said in a Telegram post.
He said that Zelensky “shamelessly lined his own pockets with American taxpayer money” under Biden, who Trump says provided Ukraine with some $350 billion in US aid. “And he kept dipping into the pot under Trump, too, taking whatever was left,” Medvedev added.
The Ukrainian “cozied up to Mexican drug cartels” by providing drone warfare training in exchange for proceeds from drug sales in the US, he alleged.
Zelensky has also “given the American president the finger” by refusing to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries despite Trump’s repeated warnings.
There is a growing rift between Trump and Zelensky over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries. The US president has demanded that Ukraine stop, accusing it of exacerbating the global fuel crisis and raising prices for Americans – a sensitive issue ahead of the November 3 US midterms. Kiev has thus far refused.
Zelensky has also accused Washington of temporarily restricting intelligence sharing and access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite network, which Ukraine uses for battlefield communications and drone operations.
To ease the fuel crisis, Trump temporarily waived sanctions on Russian fuel exports as part of a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Under the agreement, Moscow agreed to supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, another 500,000 tons in November and further shipments thereafter. The first three tankers carrying Russian diesel are already heading across the Atlantic, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Friday.

articles.title: Trump rules out Sunday strike on Iran as Netanyahu warns Israel faces imminent existential threat
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump said Sunday that the United States would not launch a military strike against Iran today.
Asked by a reporter whether a US attack on Iran could take place as soon as today, Trump replied: “Would I tell you that? The answer is no. There will not be a strike today.”
The president did not rule out military action at a later date.
Earlier on Sunday, Trump told reporters that he has yet to make a decision on whether or not to renew strikes against Iran.
“Should I finish the job - which would be very easy to do - or should I reach an agreement? That is the whole decision," he said.
Trump says 'not much going on' at Iranian nuclear sites, Netanyahu claims Israel facing existential threat
Trump added that the US is actively monitoring activity at Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site as well as three other sites that were allegedly destroyed in previous strikes.
“There isn’t much activity going on there,” he clarified.
Trump’s comments came after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed in a post on X/Twitter that Israel is currently facing “real and tangible existential danger” coming from Iran.
Netanyahu claimed that only a small window of time remains for Israel and the US to act and completely defeat Iran.
Netanyahu also shared a video from one of the IDF's anti-missile batteries where he said: "The IDF is prepared on both defense and in offense. I warn our enemies – you will absorb strikes out of proportion, stronger than you can even imagine."
Trump said on Friday that Washington is weighing another military operation against Iran, saying that the US “may do another little Epic Fury” during a pre-midterm election rally in Florida.
US-Israeli strike on Iran: Not if, when
Additionally, US officials believe that a joint US-Israeli strike on Iran is not a question of “if,” but “when.”
“It appears that Trump has decided he wants to carry out a significant strike against Iran. The only question is when to do it,” one official told The Jerusalem Post.
Another official said the president was “very close” to escalating US action against Iran.
The prevailing assessment in Washington is that Trump will hold off on making a final decision on military action against Iran until after the November 3 midterm elections.
On Sunday, Trump told Fox News in an interview: “I have a decision to make: Do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal? That's the decision.”

articles.title: Russia Targets Epicentr Stores Across Four Cities in Under 24 Hours
articles.body:
Russian forces targeted shopping centers belonging to the Epicentr retail network across Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, Vinnytsia, and Poltava in under 24 hours, company officials and regional authorities reported on Sunday, Oct. 25.
Head of Epicentr’s Public Relations Department Yuliia Chudnovets announced on Facebook that the commercial chain had been subjected to a coordinated sequence of aerial strikes across central, southern, and eastern Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, Vinnytsia, Poltava. Again in less than 24 hours,” Chudnovets stated, characterizing the concerted bombardment as a campaign aimed at the total destruction of the retail network’s infrastructure.
The corporate statement follows Sunday morning strikes in Poltava, where a strike drone hit an Epicentr hypermarket building, igniting an immediate fire, causing structural damage, and injuring a 52-year-old woman, according to Poltava Regional Military Administration Head Vitalii Diakivnych.
Multi-city strikes and double-tap attack in Kharkiv
The targeting of the Poltava hypermarket forms part of a synchronized assault against commercial retail hubs across multiple regional centers.
In Kharkiv’s Osnovianskyi district, Russian munitions engaged commercial facilities in a double-tap attack. Initial reports indicate that Russian forces launched a missile at the commercial center, followed by a secondary strike within a minute of the first impact. The strikes wounded a 39-year-old man and ignited an extensive structural fire across the commercial premises.
Russia Launche 1,600 Bombs and 2,300 Drones Over Past Week
Concurrently over the weekend, strikes hit commercial trade facilities in Zaporizhzhia, damaging retail sites and adjacent vehicles, while infrastructure and residential quarters were engaged during a drone barrage across Vinnytsia region.
The coordinated wave against Epicentr centers coincided with broader strikes on commercial and municipal logistics, including the overnight destruction of an emergency fire-tanker truck in Kharkiv during secondary strikes on first responders and an attack on a warehouse in Lozova that killed a 45-year-old commercial employee.
Pattern of commercial retail interdiction
Ukrainian municipal authorities and retail operators have repeatedly emphasized that systematic standoff strikes directed against large-scale construction hypermarkets, civilian shopping hubs, and logistics warehouses serve no military objective.
Epicentr hypermarkets function as primary commercial centers for building supplies, consumer goods, and municipal repair materials utilized by local populations and utility services to restore homes and infrastructure following aerial bombardments.

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine report deaths and injuries in overnight strikes
articles.body:
At least three people were killed and 16 injured in Ukrainian attacks on Russia, while 10 people were injured in Russian strikes on Ukraine, officials from both countries said on Sunday.
In Russia, two people were killed and two seriously injured in a Ukrainian drone attack on a minibus belonging to an agricultural enterprise in the village of Borshchovo in the Bryansk region, regional head Yegor Kovalchuk said.
In Belgorod, one person was killed and 14 injured in a large-scale overnight drone attack, regional Governor Alexander Shuvaev said on the Russian social media platform Max.
In Ukraine, 10 people, including three emergency responders, were injured in Russian strikes in Kharkiv and Vinnytsia, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said.
Six more people were injured in a Russian strike on a residential five-story building in Vinnytsia, it added.
The attacks sparked fires, and emergency crews came under repeated strikes while responding to the incidents, the service said.
A fire engine tanker was completely destroyed, it added.
Meanwhile, Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces continued overnight strikes against logistics centers, port infrastructure facilities in Ukraine and vessels allegedly carrying supplies for Ukrainian forces.
In Kharkiv, Russian strikes hit the Epicentr logistics center, a distribution center and the Vasyshchevo logistics terminal, it said.
According to the ministry, the facilities were used to store military or dual-use goods intended to support Ukraine's armed forces.
The ministry also claimed that a dry cargo vessel carrying supplies for Ukrainian forces was struck while crossing the sea en route to the port of Chornomorsk.
Russian air defences intercepted and destroyed 532 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over 25 Russian regions overnight, the ministry said.
The claims from both sides could not be independently verified.

articles.title: Ukrainian Company F-Drones Develops Low-Cost F-Jet 80 Interceptor to Counter Shaheds
articles.body:
Ukrainian company F-Drones is developing the F-Jet 80, a jet-powered interceptor drone designed to counter Russian jet-powered strike drones.
The New York Times reported this.
The new drone is being positioned as a low-cost interception system, with a target price of around $7,000.
To improve accuracy, engineers plan to equip the interceptor with artificial intelligence to help detect and pursue aerial targets.
In comments to Militarnyi, the developers said the project aims to create an interceptor powered by a compact jet engine producing 8-10 kgf of thrust.
One of the main development challenges is keeping the drone’s cost low. The developers aim to keep the price between $5,000 and $7,000 to enable simple, mass production.
Thanks to its jet engine, the F-Jet 80 is intended to counter Russian Geran-type jet-powered drones.
According to Ihor, an engineer-designer at the company, the drone has already intercepted and destroyed several targets.
Russia is expanding its use of jet-powered strike drones in its war against Ukraine. Traditional kamikaze drones powered by internal combustion engines fly relatively slowly, making them easy targets for Ukrainian interceptor drones.
Jet engines allow drones to fly faster and pass through areas covered by air defense systems more quickly.
Militarnyi previously reported that Russia had increased production of Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered strike drones to 4,000 units per month. This is twice the production volume of piston-powered Geran-2 drones.
Meanwhile, intelligence data indicate that Russia produces around 2,000 piston-powered Geran-2 drones each month.
