articles.title: Netanyahu warns of sanctions, opponents warn of collapse: Who's scaring voters? - analysis
articles.body:
In the wake of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s comments on Friday about the possibility of using cryptocurrency to bypass economic sanctions, one thing is clear: someone is engaging in fearmongering just a few days before the election.
The question is: Who is trying to frighten whom?
Is it Netanyahu trying to frighten the public? At least that was the instant interpretation of some pundits after he discussed the matter on Friday in an interview with economic journalist Roy Katz on the Channel 10 economic program.
But the full context matters.
Katz asked whether Netanyahu was worried about the day after US President Donald Trump. Netanyahu answered, “Tell me, you’re not worried?”
After saying that the billions of dollars in US military aid would soon come to an end because the US had changed, Netanyahu added that Israel needed to understand that sanctions, including banking sanctions, were possible.
“So you need to organize a bypass economy,” Netanyahu said. “You know, there are currencies that can bypass (sanctions). We are also working on that.”
In looking at those comments, it is important to distinguish between what Netanyahu said and what was subsequently attributed to him.
He did not present a crypto economy as his preferred option. He presented it as a contingency plan in the drawer for that rainy day.
Preparing for such contingencies is part of a government’s job. It does not mean that Jerusalem has thrown up its hands, resigned itself to widespread sanctions, and begun planning to disconnect Israel from the global economy.
It means that if the country faces not a rainy day but a deluge of sanctions, the government wants something in the drawer to try to bypass them.
Whether that something would work is a legitimate question. But it is a different question from whether Netanyahu wants to lead Israel into economic isolation.
'Bibicoin' a threat to national security
Because Netanyahu’s campaigns have long warned of the diplomatic and military dangers awaiting the country if voters fail to support Likud, many in the media immediately saw this as the familiar pattern: he was scaring the public again.
But it was not exactly clear how telling voters that Israel could face economic isolation after years under Netanyahu’s leadership was supposed to draw them to his side. What was clear, however, was the frightening picture his opponents painted in response.
Yashar party head Gadi Eisenkot called the “Bibicoin vision” a threat to national security – inflating a remark about a contingency plan into a full-blown vision.
“After he finished dismantling Israeli society and weakening the IDF, Netanyahu has marked the next target: the dismantling of the Israeli economy for generations to come.”
Marked the next target? Netanyahu spoke about preparing for possible sanctions. Eisenkot turned that into an intention to dismantle the economy.
And then came the warning that if Netanyahu’s “vision” were implemented, “Israelis will lose their pensions and all their investments, and many of them will leave the country.”
Talk about trying to scare the voters.
Naftali Bennett, too, got into the act, not to be outdone by his rival in the change bloc.
“In [Netanyahu’s] view, Israel will become a withdrawn and outcast country in the world, disconnected from the economy, academia, and the global technology, so that we will be forced to move to a crypto and isolated economy,” he said.
The problem is that this is not what Netanyahu said. He did not say this was the future he wanted, or even that it would happen. He said Israel needed to prepare in case sanctions were imposed.
Those statements are quite different. The opposition’s responses simply erased what was originally said.
Bank of Israel says cryptocurrencies cannot circumvent sanctions
The Bank of Israel also weighed in, giving the controversy the added authority of the country’s central bank. It said cryptocurrencies could not be used to circumvent sanctions.
That is a substantive objection. If the proposed contingency plan cannot work, the public should know.
But the bank did not stop there.
“The right course for the Israeli economy is to maintain economic relations with our primary trading partners and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy,” its statement said. “This is the responsibility of the political leadership, and it should act upon it.”
Of course that is the right course. But who said otherwise?
By setting out that course as a corrective to Netanyahu’s remarks, the bank lent weight to the impression that he had proposed abandoning it: that instead of maintaining Israel’s economic ties and preventing sanctions, the prime minister was preparing to retreat into a crypto economy.
Yet saying that the government is working on a contingency plan does not mean it has raised the white flag on sanctions. Nor does it mean that Israel will stop working diplomatically to prevent them.
Then came a group of 109 senior economists, the Economists’ Forum for Democracy, which emerged from the 2023 protests against the judicial reforms, with a warning that banking sanctions would bring something approaching economic apocalypse.
This, they said, would pertain to soaring unemployment, the disappearance of foreign investment, a collapse in Israel’s global economic standing, unusable credit cards, no access to online retailers such as Amazon, and a mass departure of foreign workers unable to send money home.
And Netanyahu was the one accused of frightening the public.
The consequences of sweeping banking sanctions would plainly be serious. But discussing a fallback plan does not mean Netanyahu is announcing that sanctions are coming, much less choosing to bring them about, and presenting his remarks that way is itself peddling fear.
None of this requires accepting that Netanyahu is above doing the same to win votes. Those looking for examples need not look far.
On Sunday, he shared an AI-generated image on X/Twitter depicting a nuclear explosion over Tel Aviv, alongside a post by right-wing commentator Yuval Bloomberg warning that failing to elect a leader capable of confronting Iran could risk a “second Holocaust.”
A nuclear explosion over Tel Aviv. A second Holocaust. Days before an election.
That is fearmongering, and it deserves to be called out.
But so does taking a contingency plan, calling it a vision, and warning voters that it will cost them their pensions, their investments, and their access to AliExpress.
The opposition has enough real examples of Netanyahu’s fearmongering without manufacturing another, and then engaging in its own version of spreading fear.

articles.title: Could Hormuz become America’s Suez?
articles.body:
In 1956, Britain was forced to abandon the Suez Canal and withdraw from Egypt after a humiliating political and financial defeat. The crisis did not end the British Empire overnight, but it exposed the decline of a power that had dominated much of the world for more than two centuries, in an empire on which the sun famously never set. Britain could still fight wars, but it could no longer act as an independent global power without facing the economic and political limits of its strength. Now, nearly seventy years later, the question is whether the war with Iran and the crisis around the Strait of Hormuz could become America’s Suez.
When war becomes too expensive
After Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal in July 1956, Britain, France and Israel launched a military campaign to regain control of the canal and weaken Nasser’s government. Their forces made rapid progress, but the operation soon became a financial and political crisis for London.
The British pound came under heavy pressure, and the Bank of England had to use its dollar reserves to defend the currency. The United States opposed the invasion and refused to provide the financial support Britain needed unless it agreed to stop the operation. On 6th November, Britain accepted a ceasefire. It later withdrew its forces from Egypt.
As the International Monetary Fund’s account of the crisis explains, the pressure on sterling was central to Britain’s decision. The crisis showed that the government could not continue the war without putting its financial position at long-term risk.
The war with Iran could create a similar problem for the United States, although the economic conditions are different. The dollar is far stronger internationally than the pound was in 1956, and the American economy has greater resources. But the comparison is about the cost of sustaining a war when its political goals remain out of reach.
If the war continues without a clear result, the United States will have to spend more on military operations, weapons, logistics and the protection of its forces. At the same time, the disruption of energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz can raise costs across the global economy. These pressures may gradually make the war harder to justify, especially if Iran can draw the United States into a prolonged conflict with no clear progress toward its goals.
The cost reaches American households
The Strait of Hormuz is central to this problem because of its role in the global energy market. Before the war, around one-fifth of the world’s oil consumption passed through the strait, along with a major share of global liquefied natural gas shipments. As oil prices rose, gasoline and diesel became more expensive, air travel and shipping costs increased, and the cost of transporting goods went up. This is where the war became a serious domestic problem for the White House. Higher gasoline prices were immediately visible to American households. Families had to spend more to drive for daily activities and higher diesel prices increased the cost of moving goods.
The latest energy-market reports show how difficult this problem can even become. In October 2026, Reuters reported that Brent crude remained above $100 a barrel. Diesel prices in the United States had also risen sharply, adding to domestic political pressure ahead of the midterm elections. The Reuters report on rising oil prices and the prolonged conflict describes the growing challenge for the Trump administration.
High energy prices can also make it harder to control inflation. Transport and production become more expensive, and the effects spread through the economy. If the Federal Reserve keeps interest rates high to control inflation, borrowing becomes more expensive for households and businesses. The government also has to meet the direct cost of the war while paying interest on its existing debt.
Nevertheless, none of these pressures would force Washington to end the war. The key issue is their combined effect over time. If the war continues, energy prices remain high and the United States fails to achieve objectives, the economic cost of continuing may eventually become greater than the expected benefit.
From military leverage to economic limits
A war of attrition changes the way governments calculate success. At the beginning of a conflict, leaders may expect military action to produce a quick political result. If that result does not come, they face a difficult choice: increase the pressure and spend more, or accept that the original goals may be impossible to achieve at an acceptable cost.
This is the danger facing the United States. Washington has the ability to strike Iranian targets and maintain a strong military presence in the region. But the ability to damage does not mean that Iran will accept American demands. If each new round of fighting adds to the cost without producing a decisive political result, the United States will find itself spending more while moving no closer to its goals.
The Strait of Hormuz gives Iran a way to increase this pressure. Disruption to shipping can keep energy markets unstable and raise the economic cost of the conflict well beyond the battlefield. The longer the disruption continues, the more difficult it becomes for Washington to separate its military campaign from its effects on the American economy.
The question is whether the United States can continue to bear the full cost of the conflict if the economic pressure grows while the chance of achieving its objectives declines. At some stage, American administration may conclude that continuing the war will bring more damage than benefit. That would create the conditions for an American retreat. If Washington withdraws without achieving its main goals, the result could be a strategic defeat, even if American forces remain far stronger than Iran’s in conventional military terms.
Why China could benefit
Such an outcome would also affect the wider balance of power. China is already benefiting from a war that consumes American resources, damages Washington’s reputation and reduces its ability to focus on other strategic priorities. Beijing does not need to defeat the United States directly. It can benefit simply by watching Americas useless overstretch. The war also gives China an opportunity to question whether the United States can keep its commitments to allies in Asia. China would also suffer from high energy prices and disruptions to trade. But if the United States emerges from the war with fewer resources, greater economic pressure and damaged credibility, China could gain room to expand its influence without taking on the costs of a direct military confrontation.
This is one reason the outcome of the war matters beyond the Middle East. A costly American withdrawal could affect how allies and rivals judge US power. Countries that depend on Washington for security may question its ability to sustain a long conflict. Rivals may become more willing to challenge American influence in other regions.
Could this be America’s Suez?
The Suez Crisis did not single-handedly end British power. Britain’s relative decline had been developing for decades, and the United States had already become the leading Western power. But Suez made the change unmistakable. Britain had launched a heavy military operation and then had to withdraw under financial and political pressure. But the crisis clearly exposed the limits of its ability to act as a global power.
A similar outcome is possible for the United States in Iran. If the war becomes more costly with time, if energy prices continue to place pressure on American households and businesses, and if Washington cannot achieve its main objectives, the economic logic for continuing the conflict may become increasingly weak. A withdrawal without a clear political achievement would then damage the credibility of American power as a world superpower.
The United States is not Britain in 1956. Its international position will not collapse because of one war. Yet these advantages do not remove the basic problem: US may ruin its credit as super power of current international order.
The real test will come when Washington has to choose between continuing an expensive war and accepting a retreat. If it leaves Iran without achieving its goals, the consequences could extend far beyond the battlefield. The war could become a turning point that speeds up the decline of American order and gives other powers more room to shape the coming international order. Such scenario would be what could make Hormuz America’s Suez.

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition says it downed 2 missiles fired by Houthis
articles.body:
(Reuters) -- Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis said they launched attacks on Saudi oil facilities and airports on Saturday, and the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group said it downed two missiles, as clashes between the two sides intensified.
On another front of an escalating conflict reignited by the Iran war, Yemen's Saudi-backed government said the Houthis also fired three ballistic missiles at coast guard sites in the southern Yemeni port city of Aden.
Saudi authorities did not comment directly on the Houthi statements, though they reported missile debris falling near the site of one of the purported oil targets. It was not immediately clear if any of the reported attacks had hit their targets in the kingdom or had been intercepted.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery, crude oil pumping stations and the East-West Pipeline.
He also said the group targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, an airport in Najran and an airbase in Khamis Mushait.
The Saudi-led coalition earlier said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by Houthis towards Yanbu and Taif.
Saudi Civil Defense said debris from intercepted missiles had fallen in the Mecca and Medina regions, home to Islam's holiest sites visited by millions of Muslim pilgrims every year.
It said parts of the intercepted missiles fell in Wadi al-Mughammas in Mecca, while debris also fell in areas in Jeddah, Taif and Rabigh. It was not clear if that was linked to the Houthis' reported targeting of the Rabigh oil refinery.
Shortly after that, Houthis denied that they attacked Mecca and Medina, saying that their operations "target Saudi oil facilities and military bases."
The renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce that largely halted cross-border attacks between the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen's internationally recognized government, and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa.
The escalation has opened another front in the US-Israeli war on Iran.
In Yemen, the Interior Ministry of the internationally recognized government said two of the Houthis' missiles had struck a coast guard headquarters, while a third hit a coast guard building in the Tawahi district.
Houthi spokesman Saree said the group's forces had targeted Saudi-backed military gatherings at what he called Al-Nasr camp and a naval base in Aden, saying Saudi officers were overseeing the mobilization there.
There was no immediate comment from the Saudi-led coalition on that assertion.
Earlier on Saturday, Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense briefly issued alerts warning residents of potential danger in Taif and Yanbu, as well as in the holy city of Mecca and the kingdom's second-largest city, Jeddah.
About 10 minutes later, the agency said the threat had passed.
The Houthis warned airlines earlier this month against using Saudi airspace, exempting only the airspace over Mecca and Medina, as they intensified attacks on the kingdom.

articles.title: Bulgaria votes for president in election dominated by Ukraine war and the economy
articles.body:
The campaign has focused on Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and an increase in drone attacks on commercial vessels off Bulgaria's coast in the Black Sea, as well as rising energy prices and inflation.
Exit polls showed Bulgaria's current President Iliana Yotova to be narrowly ahead in the first round of the country's presidential elections on Sunday, with between 35% and 36.5% of the vote.
She is now set to face Andrey Gyurov, a banker and former caretaker prime minister, in a 1 November runoff, after he came in second with between 32.2% and 32.5%.
In the weeks leading up to the election, Yotova was expected to win between 41% and 47% of the vote, while Gyurov was polling between 28% and 31%.
Preliminary results are now expected to be published on Monday.
The election campaign has mostly revolved around growing concerns over the economy and drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea.
It is seen as the first major test of Prime Minister Rumen Radev's Progressive Bulgaria party since it came out on top in parliamentary elections last April.
President Iliana Yotova is backed by Radev's party and favours dialogue with Moscow while opposing military aid to Ukraine, and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov is backed by pro-Western opposition parties.
The campaign has focused heavily on Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the widening hostilities in the Black Sea, where recent drone attacks on commercial vessels off Bulgaria’s coast have heightened security concerns in the European Union and NATO member country.
The strikes have raised concerns over Russia’s intentions to escalate the conflict, while also compelling the government to ask Bulgaria's partners for assistance to strengthen its maritime security.
Candidates have also looked to respond to public anxiety over rising energy prices and inflation, as many families, particularly in rural areas, struggle to make ends meet.
Two main candidates among record total of 27
Main frontrunner Yotova took over this year as president of Bulgaria when Rumen Radev stepped down to run in parliamentary elections, eventually becoming prime minister.
If successful, she would become the first woman ever elected president in Bulgaria's history. A win for Yotova would be a boost for Radev, who has also called for dialogue with Moscow.
A former journalist and member of the European Parliament, Yotova was elected vice-president alongside Radev in 2016 and 2021.
Her main challenger is economist Andrey Gyurov, a former deputy governor of the central bank and caretaker prime minister in the first few months of 2026. He is supported by the pro-Western reformist opposition.
Gyurov has often expressed firm support for Ukraine, and signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his premiership.

articles.title: US updates travel warnings for 13 Middle Eastern countries
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US updates travel warnings for 13 Middle Eastern countries
The United States has updated travel advisories for 13 countries across the Middle East, citing the risk of further attacks by Yemen’s Houthis and alleged Iranian efforts to target American officials in the region. The revisions come alongside reductions in staffing at several US embassies amid concerns over a wider escalation.
The advisories, dated 23 October, cover Bahrain, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Syria, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen. The updates revise the security warnings rather than raise the countries’ existing advisory levels.
"The possibility of regional effects, including the potential for flight disruptions, makes a region-wide advisory update important and prudent," a State Department official said in comments shared by PBS correspondent Nick Schifrin.
The department said the revisions reflected increased potential for armed attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis and Iranian efforts to target US government officials. Those claims come amid renewed fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition, including missile and drone attacks on Saudi territory.
Advisories by country, and what they mean:
Eight countries are listed at Level 3, meaning Americans should reconsider travel, while five remain at Level 4 — "do not travel", the State Department’s highest warning. The country-specific warnings are:
- Bahrain: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and other security risks.
- Iran: Level 4 — Do not travel. Washington cites unrest, kidnapping or hostage-taking, terrorism, wrongful detention and other risks.
- Iraq: Level 4 — Do not travel. The advisory lists unrest, crime, health risks, kidnapping or hostage-taking, terrorism and other risks.
- Israel: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and unrest.
- Jordan: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and other security risks.
- Kuwait: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. Washington cites crime and other risks.
- Lebanon: Level 4 — Do not travel. The advisory lists unrest, crime, kidnapping or hostage-taking, terrorism and other risks.
- Oman: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and other security risks.
- Qatar: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists “other” risks, rather than a separate terrorism, crime or unrest indicator.
- Saudi Arabia: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and other security risks. The update follows Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, including the 10 October strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport.
- Syria: Level 4 — Do not travel. Washington cites unrest, crime, kidnapping or hostage-taking, terrorism and other risks.
- United Arab Emirates: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and other security risks.
- Yemen: Level 4 — Do not travel. The advisory lists unrest, crime, health risks, kidnapping or hostage-taking, terrorism and other risks.
US authorities have urged Americans to monitor embassy alerts and airline operations, prepare for possible flight cancellations or airspace closures, and maintain emergency departure plans that do not depend on US government assistance. They also recommend enrolling in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program to receive security updates.
The warnings follow Friday’s reports that Washington was reducing staffing at its embassies in Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar and the UAE. Axios first reported an intelligence memo alleging that Iranian plots against American personnel had reached "advanced stages"; the Associated Press subsequently obtained the memo and confirmed the staffing reductions with US officials.
Those four embassies remain open under restricted operations, and personnel are not subject to the same compulsory departure order issued on Wednesday for non-essential US staff and their families in Saudi Arabia.
US officials have denied that the staffing changes are linked to prospective new US or Israeli strikes on Iran. The advisory updates themselves do not establish that another military operation is imminent, although the move comes amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, with US ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack warning that Washington could "absolutely" strike Iran before the upcoming US midterm elections.

articles.title: Iran fears only Netanyahu. On Tuesday, make sure it stays that way - opinion
articles.body:
Here is a question: Imagine social media had been around in the early 1930s. What would Winston Churchill's political rivals have said if he had posted images of German troops marching across Europe, warning of what was to come?
Well, he didn’t have social media, but he did sound the alarm.
Churchill warned of the threat of Hitler in a speech to the British Parliament a mere two months after Hitler came to power. The response? His opponents labeled him a warmonger, his remarks dismissed as hysteria.
On Sunday, Benjamin Netanyahu shared an AI image of an Iranian nuclear bomb exploding in Tel Aviv. His principal rival, Gadi Eisenkot, called him “hysterical” and accused him of using “lies and scare tactics”.
Eisenkot might have said the same about Churchill in 1933. History proved that the danger then was not imaginary and that Churchill was right. Very, very right.
Benjamin Netanyahu is today’s Churchill at a time when Israel faces a threat which, in my opinion, is many times greater than Europe faced with Hitler in 1939. We know, tragically, the Holocaust happened before Nazi Germany was defeated. But Israel rose out of its ashes.
This time, more than seven million Jews - and two million Arabs - face annihilation, and, hit by an Iranian nuclear bomb, Israel will not come back again.
The very existence of our country is at stake, and only one man can save it. This is not hyperbole. Gadi Eisenkot dismisses Netanyahu's nuclear warning as political histrionics.
Alternative choices to Netanyahu are one and the same
Eisenkot’s allies offer little reassurance either. Naftali Bennett has already shown his willingness to lead a government which included the left-wing Meretz and the Islamist Ra'am.
Avigdor Lieberman for years supported a two-state solution involving handing over territory. And Yair Golan? Here is a would-be prime minister who suggested that Israel killed babies in Gaza "as a hobby"!
Why do I mention these names? Because they are the alternative choice to Netanyahu when Israelis go to the polls on Tuesday. Vote for one and you vote for them all.
They are the Change Bloc - an assortment that has only one thing in common: ousting Bibi. That objective is their only common ground. Not policy. Not ideology. Not the direction of Israel’s future. Just toppling one man. Beyond that, chaos.
We have witnessed what happens when chaos and division ensue. Hamas saw the demonstrations, the incitement, the refusals to serve in the IDF, the appearance of Israel as vulnerable. The result was October 7th.
Who was behind the protests? The same forces trying to bring Bibi down today. The same forces who do not see the writing on the wall. The same forces who think Netanyahu is a greater threat to Israel than Iran. This is delusional, and it is fatal.
Had Iran had the chance, Israel would not be here now. Believe Iranian leaders when they say they want to destroy us. It did not end with the elimination of Khamenei.
On the contrary, Iran is more determined than ever to get its hands on a nuclear bomb. It is already rebuilding its nuclear facilities and will recover the enriched uranium - currently buried under rubble thanks to US and Israeli strikes - needed for a weapon.
It is only a matter of time. Netanyahu knows this, and only Netanyahu can stop this. Netanyahu is the reason why Iran has not yet managed to build a nuclear bomb. Netanyahu saw the writing on the wall, 30 years ago. He was the Churchill of the day then, and he still is now.
If Iran gets the bomb, no amount of street protests will make it disappear. Political differences will not make it disappear. Neither will arguments about the cost of living or judicial reform.
Iran does not fear Eisenkot, Bennett, Lieberman or Golan. Iran only fears Netanyahu. If you care about Israel, if you care about your children, and if you care about your grandchildren, when you vote on Tuesday, make sure it stays that way.

articles.title: FP-1 drones traveled more than 2,500 km and struck two facilities in Omsk: the "Omsk Rubber" plant and an OZON warehouse were hit
articles.body:
FP-1 drones traveled more than 2,500 km and struck two facilities in Omsk: the "Omsk Rubber" plant and an OZON warehouse were hit
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian FP-1 drones traveled more than 2,500 km and struck the "Omsk Rubber" plant and an OZON warehouse in Omsk. The plant accounts for about 25% of rubber production in the Russian Federation.
Ukrainian long-range FP-1 drones struck two sites at once in Russia’s Omsk on the evening of October 24, covering more than 2,500 km from the border. The targets were Omsk Rubber, one of the largest petrochemical plants in the Russian Federation, and the logistics warehouse complex of the OZON marketplace. UNN reports this, citing the company’s Telegram channel, Fire Point, the drone manufacturer.
Details
The FP-1 drones covered more than 2,500 km from the border and struck two sites at once in Omsk
Fire Point said that the Defense Forces attacked the Omsk Rubber plant, one of the largest petrochemical enterprises in the Russian Federation. According to previously published data, the enterprise accounted for about 25% of Russia’s production of butadiene-styrene rubbers.
The logistics warehouse complex of OZON was also traditionally targeted
Denys Shtilerman, co-owner and chief designer of Fire Point, also reposted the moment of the strike in Omsk, which was published on "X".
Additionally
The night before, on October 24, FP-1 drones struck another enterprise in the Russian Federation’s rubber industry - the Tolyattikauchuk plant in the Samara region, which, according to Fire Point, accounts for about 25% of the Russian synthetic rubber market. The plant’s products are used in the production of Russian weapons, including ballistic missiles.
Omsk, located more than 2,500 km from the border, has not been targeted by FP-1 drones for the first time: previously, they attacked the Omsk Oil Refinery, the largest oil refinery in the Russian Federation, several times, most recently on October 8.

articles.title: Putin’s residence in Valdai has been surrounded by a second ring of air defenses — the number of positions has exceeded 50
articles.body:
Putin’s residence in Valdai has been surrounded by a second ring of air defenses — the number of positions has exceeded 50
Kyiv • UNN
More than 50 air defense positions have been identified within a 50-kilometer radius of Putin’s residence. In October alone, 15 new towers appeared on the Ukrainian side.
A second air defense ring has been built around the residence of Russian dictator Vladimir Putin in Valdai. There are already more than 50 air defense positions within a 50-kilometer radius of the estate. The Moscow Times reports this, citing satellite imagery, writes UNN.
Details
In October alone, more than 15 new towers for deploying Pantsir or Tor anti-aircraft systems appeared south of the residence, on the side facing Ukraine.
Since April, the number of air defense positions around the estate has doubled. For comparison, in Moscow and the Moscow region, where more than 20 million people live, only approximately twice as many such positions were built after the start of the full-scale invasion.
The Kremlin strengthens security around the residence
At the end of December 2025, Russia accused Ukraine of allegedly attacking Putin's residence with 91 drones. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called these claims fake.
After this, the Russian authorities began strengthening security at the site. In particular, in the summer, anti-drone nets began to be installed over the road leading to the residence.
According to journalistic investigations, Putin and his close associates had regularly used the residence in the past, but recently may have stopped traveling there due to concerns for their own safety.

articles.title: Ukrainian drones reportedly strike major shopping mall in Russia’s Belgorod overnight
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces reportedly struck the MegaGRINN shopping and entertainment complex in the Russian city of Belgorod during a mass drone attack overnight on 25 October, when the mall was closed and no visitors were inside, according to the Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+.
Russian authorities reported that a civilian was killed and 10 people were injured in the broader mass drone attack on Belgorod. One of the injured was an ambulance worker, according to the regional operational headquarters.
The majority of the drones reportedly targeted one area in the city center, according to ASTRA.
Belgorod’s largest shopping complex targeted
Exilenova+ identified the reported target as MegaGRINN, Belgorod’s largest shopping and entertainment complex covering about 163,000 square meters. The facility houses more than 200 stores, a supermarket, restaurants, a cinema, and entertainment areas.
Belgorod is a Russian city about 34 kilometers (21 miles) from Ukraine’s northeastern border and roughly 70 kilometers (43 miles) from Kharkiv. The city and surrounding oblast have repeatedly come under Ukrainian drone attacks during Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine.
Belgorod Oblast borders Ukraine’s Sumy, Kharkiv, and Luhansk oblasts. Russian forces have used the region to launch missile and drone attacks on Ukraine and to stage ground offensives across the border.
Update: Ukraine’s General Staff reports strikes on Russian radar stations in Belgorod Oblast
Update 18:00: Ukraine’s General Staff said Ukrainian forces struck Russian radar stations near Hostishchevo and Kurgannoye in Russia’s Belgorod Oblast on 24 October and overnight on 25 October.
The General Staff said the strikes would create gaps in Russian radar coverage and expand Ukraine’s ability to use unmanned systems.
The update did not mention an attack on Belgorod city or the shopping mall.
Russia steps up attacks on Ukrainian retail infrastructure
The reported strike comes amid an intensified Russian campaign against Ukrainian retail and logistics infrastructure. These attacks have included strikes on shopping centers during business hours, including a 21 August Russian drone attack on the crowded Soniachna Halereia mall in Kryvyi Rih, where 16 people were killed and more than 120 injured.
The reported strike on MegaGRINN took place overnight, when the complex was reportedly closed and empty of visitors. Russian authorities reported casualties from the wider attack on Belgorod, but have not linked them to the mall.

articles.title: 'Missiles from Iran': Facebook, TikTok and Instagram feed us scary news from the past
articles.body:
On Sunday, June 7, late in the evening, Iran attacked Israel. The Israel Defense Forces spokesman quickly released a video: "A short while ago, the Iranian terror regime launched missiles toward the territory of the State of Israel." Across the country, Israelis rushed to tidy up their bomb shelters and braced for another sleepless night.
Two weeks later, Erez was checking his Instagram feed one morning when he came across a video. On screen: the same IDF spokesman, the same posture, the same alarming tone — and the same announcement, word for word. No date appeared on screen; without checking, there was no telling it was the same old video. It looked entirely current.
Another three weeks went by. Avi was scrolling through TikTok and saw it too: the same spokesman, the same message. On September 5, Ayelet saw it as well — 90 days after it was first posted.
In reality, the event happened once. But on social media, the algorithm kept showing users reruns of the emergency announcement, which kept racking up views. As far as the recommendation system was concerned, that's what users wanted.
Recycled war declarations, weeks-old terror attacks raised from the dead, old updates about looming attacks from Home Front Command and other anxiety-inducing posts pulled up from the digital archive are part of a worsening phenomenon on social media, now the main way for people to communicate. One way to put it: Tech companies have erased time, or at least obscured it, pushing old content in the so-called news feed while also hiding the date and hindering the ability to actually check when a post was first posted. And when we lose our grasp of time, a frightening past can come back to haunt us.
A Haaretz digital investigation, based on an analysis of tens of thousands of posts and videos from the Facebook, Instagram and TikTok accounts of six digital personas created for this purpose, points to hundreds of cases in which the algorithm re-served old, anxiety-inducing news, the vast majority on Facebook and TikTok. Many videos carry no visible date, and real users struggled to tell when they were posted. Their comments say as much: "Is this from today???"; "Not again 💔"; "Why cause unnecessary panic"; "Panicked, I thought it was now"; "It would be nice if you put a date on these videos"; "Why. Is. There. No. Date. On. The. Video."
A sample of headlines from the personas' feeds: "Incident has not ended: Shooting attack in Sharon region — cruel murder spree in several locations" (a news site's video, shown 73 days after the attack); "Cleared for publication: Four soldiers killed in Lebanon" (appeared 87 days after the soldiers were killed); "Hezbollah launched rockets toward Nahariya for the first time in weeks" (47 days later); "Initial report: Our forces have begun a wave of strikes in Iran" (64 days later); "Cleared by the censor: Impacts in Karmiel area" (71 days later); "Iranian threat against Israel: 'We will respond decisively and painfully — tonight, look to the skies'" (39 days after the threat). The investigation pins down a phenomenon users noticed but struggled to put their finger on.
The process that led to this point did not happen overnight. Mundane technical changes — part of an economic battle between tech giants worth hundreds of billions of dollars — gradually added up to a phenomenon that is undermining how we perceive reality.
First, the platforms invested heavily in getting people to make and watch videos, and it paid off: Short videos became a cultural phenomenon. Brands and marketers use them to sell products; political campaigners, including in the current election, make content tailored to the format (the prime minister stands out in particular); news outlets worldwide realized that to survive, they had to join the game. Viewing data show a rapid, broad rise in video consumption. No wonder the "clip economy" has become a hallmark of the era.
Second, the same platforms — chiefly Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube — hid or removed timestamps from their videos, branded Reels, Shorts or, in TikTok's case, simply Videos. That lets them serve content untethered from chronology and tailored mainly to users' preferences, raising both the potential for addiction and time spent on the platform. Want to know when the clip you're watching was posted? Often, the date is hidden. On TikTok, researchers have had to build special tools to find it.
It's not just the videos. The platforms have undermined our sense of time in many ways. The feed went from chronological to algorithmic. This is also true for comments which are now by default, sorted by relevance, not date. On Instagram and Facebook, timestamps provide a retrospective perspective that becomes more complex as you scroll back: "13 weeks ago," "a year ago." When exactly was something posted? It's hard to say. But the biggest shift came with short video, which the apps push aggressively. Those are techniques TikTok perfected to deepen users' addiction. Their spread to other platforms is the TikTokification of the information we consume.
This has consequences. This year, for the first time, social media narrowly overtook TV and news websites as a news source globally, according to the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism at the University of Oxford. Studies also link greater exposure to security content on social media to higher anxiety. Haaretz's findings add to a growing body of evidence that the way tech giants choose to build social media platforms may harm users' mental health.
Here is another way to think about it. Imagine opening a newspaper with no date anywhere. The stories, it turns out, come from different times — some from today, some from last week, some six months old. And the headline about the war resuming? We won't tell you when it's from. Feel free to guess.
The TikTokification of platforms
Social media has metamorphosed over the years. Facebook arrived early in the millennium as a place to connect with friends and share photos and updates. Twitter, now X, followed as a text-based network; Instagram laid claim to the photo-sharing crown. Then, in 2017, TikTok was born, betting it all on video.
TikTok, owned by China's ByteDance, has gone furthest in erasing time. Its model rests on short videos, many without a visible date: fast, frenetic, filling the screen, each swipe rewarding the user with another. On the surface, it's entertainment. But studies describe a process that erodes the human capacity to make sound decisions and resist harmful impulses. Some parts of the app show a timestamp, but the default For You feed lets users scroll for hours with no sign that they have sunk into the past. Indeed, a European Commission investigation has preliminarily found that TikTok's design encourages addiction in breach of EU law.
"The rise of TikTok since 2017 is perhaps the main social media story of the last decade," the Reuters Institute's Digital News Report says. "It is also the story of a video format that has shaped how people think of online content." Industry leaders have said as much. "People have a lot of choices for how they want to spend their time, and apps like TikTok are growing very quickly," Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg told investors in 2022, adding: "This is why our focus on Reels is so important over the long term." Meta owns Facebook and Instagram, used daily by 64 and 58 percent of Israelis, respectively, according to the Israel Internet Association; TikTok, by 34 percent.
This is how everything unfolded: Instagram introduced Reels, its version of TikTok's hit short-video format, as early as 2019; YouTube launched Shorts a year later. In mid-2025, Facebook announced it was moving all its video to Reels, a process it said took a few months. And like TikTok, Facebook, Instagram and YouTube all hid their videos' timestamps — just as more and more users were turning to video for information.
Meanwhile, more people are getting their news from social media: almost 60 percent of Israelis frequently do, according to an Israel Internet Association survey. Yet though the platforms are a central venue for news - which they don't produce, relying on other sources - they don't follow the rules news organizations do. The news stories that the algorithm serves up from the archive into your feed is a striking example of this.
In search of lost time
For the investigation, Haaretz created six fictitious personas modeled on Israeli archetypes; Avi, Erez and Ayelet are three of them. All six got Facebook and TikTok accounts, and four also got Instagram. They scrolled for nearly four months. Haaretz archived every post they were shown and compared each item's original publication date with the date it appeared.
The findings show that resurfacing old content is ongoing and that the platforms recycle it on a large scale, because their algorithmic feeds let them resurface popular posts. The vast majority is innocuous, from stand-up clips to cat videos. But in Israel, where many users click on the security content that regularly fills their feeds, the algorithm also resurfaced alerts about terror attacks, missile fire, assassinations, political announcements and crime — and a report about a person who committed sexual harassment.
The alarming news the algorithm resurfaced came mainly from news outlets, including Kan News, Channel 14, N12, Israel Hayom and Ynet. Recycled posts also came from bodies such as the Israel Police, the IDF and the Home Front Command, and from high-profile figures such as Yoseph Haddad.
By Haaretz's calculation, each digital persona that was created for this investigation was shown an average of two alarming videos a week. Even if this appears to be a low number of recycled scary posts, they have an effect. "It naturally puts us on high alert," says Dr. Almog Simchon, head of the Computational Social Psychology Lab at Ben-Gurion University. "When you get security news, you need to act on it in real time — go to the safe room, check on family. We want an indication, here and now, that if something happened, our loved ones are OK. You need to process the information and figure out whether it's really happening now. If not, you need to cognitively bring down the adrenaline and stress, and you can't switch the system on in an instant and then off as if everything's fine. Recovery takes longer than activation."
Even in doubt, Simchon says, the body needs to treat the signal as something that may have happened. "We don't want to see breaking news about a terrible event and instinctively think, 'This must be old, it probably has nothing to do with me.' If it does concern me, the implications are enormous. So we want to take it into account and pay attention." Resurfacing alarming information, he adds, keeps us close to events and denies us the processing that distance brings.
Users can check when a video was published by stopping on it and clicking. On Facebook, Instagram and YouTube, that reveals the date. On TikTok, it can't be done from the For You feed at the heart of the app; the determined must open the comments and find when the first one was posted.
But this has a side effect. Clicking signals to the algorithm that the content interests users, making it likelier they'll get more of it. In other words, one archived terror attack leads to another. And commenting on an old video, as users sometimes do out of anger or panic, may raise the chances it appears in their friends' feeds.
Researchers at the Israel Internet Association have a clear name for the phenomenon: false information. "One of the common manipulations in spreading disinformation is using authentic documentation of an event detached from its original context, especially the time it occurred," Nitsan Yasur, head of disinformation department at the association, says of the findings. In a study the association conducted during the first Israel-Iran war, he says, the most prominent manipulation was presenting content out of its original time frame. "The truth is only true in its time," he says. Haaretz's investigation shows that social media algorithms naturally behave much like malicious actors.
Maya Ilany, CEO of the Brandeis Institute, which deals with technology, democracy and policy, adds: "We have to remember that ultimately, these are businesses that want to make money. They care about what keeps us on their app the longest. And one of those things is anxiety." The fixes, she says, are at least theoretically simple. "Everything can be reversed. If what they did was put everything into Reels and remove the date, then just reverse it."
Some countries, she notes, have already restricted addictive features. "For example, attorneys general in the U.S. reached an agreement with Meta that includes changing the addictive design for children. In the European Union, there's legislation on what information can be collected and limits on what can be used to target users. But in Israel, there's no law requiring the companies to do this, so why would they do it here?"
More broadly, Ilany says, the preference-based algorithm creates a fragmented reality. She points to the lively debate over whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will order a strike on Iran and whether it would help him in the election — a question, she says, to weigh against the platforms' power to shape how reality is perceived. "If there's a political actor who believes a security emergency would benefit him, he doesn't even need to make it happen in reality. He can create a manipulative feed that leads many in the public to believe we're in the midst of one — and then he has achieved his goal." Meanwhile, the algorithm serving up alarming news from the past seems to be doing that on its own.
TikTok said in response: "Our recommendation system is designed to reflect each user's personal preferences, based on their interactions on the platform. We are committed to protecting election integrity in Israel through dedicated teams, proactive enforcement and advanced safeguards against misleading information, and to keeping our community safe. We do not proactively promote specific political candidates. Drawing conclusions from subjective observation of a handful of accounts, on a platform where millions of videos are posted daily, rests on a fundamentally flawed methodology."
Meta did not respond to a Haaretz's question about our findings in this context, rather responding only to our main investigation's findings.
Haaretz created six digital personas defined by attributes such as place of residence, marital status and gender, but with no political leaning. An AI system logged the posts in their feeds, recording when each was published and when it was shown — 80,000 posts in all. Because the platforms conceal timestamps, the system could date only 13,000 of them. That subset contained dozens of examples of alarming news resurfacing long after publication; a simple calculation of the phenomenon's frequency across the full dataset points to hundreds of cases. A recurring post was defined as one shown at least 14 days after its original publication. Haaretz manually checked the machine's findings. The phenomenon also showed up in real users' private accounts throughout the investigation. Some of the data was collected with the help of Bright Data.
'The Algorithm's Election' project
Investigation, database and analysis: Omer Benjakob. Data collection: Noa Dragotsky and Adi Shaham. Writing: Omer Benjakob and Yarden Michaeli. Editing: Hagit Brinker. Project editors: Yarden Zur and Avi Scharf. Visual analysis and processing: Claude Opus 4.6.

articles.title: There were 157 battles at the front over the past day – the General Staff named the hottest areas
articles.body:
There were 157 battles at the front over the past day – the General Staff named the hottest areas
Kyiv • UNN
Russian forces launched 157 attacks, most of them in the Pokrovsk direction. The enemy carried out 42 airstrikes and used 4,834 kamikaze drones.
Since the beginning of October 25, there have been 157 combat engagements at the front. Russian forces carried out the most attacks in the Pokrovsk direction, where Ukrainian defenders repelled 22 assaults. This was reported by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine in its evening briefing as of 22:00, UNN writes.
Details
During the day, the Russians launched 42 air strikes, using 142 guided aerial bombs. The occupiers also deployed 4,834 kamikaze drones and carried out 1,758 attacks on Ukrainian positions and населated areas.
In the Pokrovsk direction, fighting took place, in particular, near Sofiivka, Kucheriv Yar, Novyi Donbas, Serhiivka, and Molodetske. As of the evening, two combat engagements were still ongoing. According to preliminary data, Ukrainian troops eliminated 29 occupiers and wounded another 23.
The situation in other directions
In the Huliaipole direction, the Defense Forces repelled 13 attacks, including near Uspenske, Rizdvianka, and Dolynka.
In the Kostiantynivka direction, the General Staff recorded 11 combat engagements, two of which were still ongoing as of 22:00.

articles.title: Thousands protest against Netanyahu ahead of Israeli election (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Thousands protest against Netanyahu ahead of Israeli election (VIDEO)
A major protest against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has taken place in Tel-Aviv just days ahead of the Israeli parliamentary election on October 27.
A square outside the Museum of Art in the country’s largest city was packed on Saturday evening, with the demonstrators holding national flags and banners, reading ‘Change will come’, ‘No more Mr. Far Right Guy’ and other slogans.
The organizers of the gathering from the October Council group put the attendance at over 100,000. The police have yet to announce official figures.
Netanyahu’s main rival in the election – Yashar party chairman and former military chief of staff, Gadi Eisenkot – and other leaders of the opposition bloc have attended the rally. The crowd cheered Eisenkot’s appearance, chanting: “Who’s coming? The next prime minister.”
The October Council was formed by families of the victims of the attack on Israel by Hamas on October 7, 2023, who demand accountability from Netanuahy’s right-wing government for the failure to prevent the incursion.
Saturday’s protest, organized with the title ‘In Three Days, Vote for a State Commission of Inquiry’, is the culmination of three years of weekly rallies, according to the group.
The State Commissions of Inquiry, which are independent panels appointed by the Supreme Court, are usually set up in Israel to investigate major failures by the authorities. However, Netanyahu refused to establish such a probe into October 7, insisting that it would be biased against his government.
Reports in the US and local media claimed that the prime minister ignored warnings of the planned attack by Hamas he had received from various sources, including Israeli intelligence and the UAE and Egypt. Netanyahu has denied those claims.
A poll by public broadcaster KAN published before the start of the election silence period on Friday, suggested that Eisenkot’s opposition bloc would get 52 out of 120 in the Israeli parliament, with Netanyahu and his supporters winning 50 seats. This means that neither is likely control the Knesset outright.
Israel responded to the October 7 incursion by Hamas, in which 1,200 people lost their lives and around 250 were taken hostage, by launching a military campaign in Gaza.
Israeli airstrikes and a ground offensive have killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, including at least 21,000 children, and injured over 175,000 others in the enclave over the past three years, according to the local Health Ministry. More than 1,500 deaths happened after a US-brokered ceasefire went into effect in October 2025.

articles.title: “Strasbourg Calling”: Europe must produce the right things, not simply more
articles.body:
Author
Irina Nedeva
Interview
German MEP from the Greens Danie Freund:
“Strasbourg Calling”: Europe must produce the right things, not simply more
Interview with MEP Daniel Freund
Sunday 25 October 2026 13:06
Sunday, 25 October 2026, 13:06
MEP Daniel Freund
PHOTO Irina Nedeva
Font size
At its Strasbourg session this week, the European Parliament discussed the conclusions of last week's European Council meeting. However, the major issue of the EU's long-term budget for 2028-2034 remains unresolved. Europe wants to become a geopolitical power, rearm, compete with China and maintain its climate targets. But who will pay for it all?
German Green MEP Daniel Freund, the Greens' coordinator on the Committee on Budgetary Control, warns that Europe cannot take on more responsibilities with less money and must not abandon its climate targets.
Speaking on BNR's special  broadcast from Strasbourg, he said:
“Europe still has a great deal to do in terms of defence, support for Ukraine and competition with China. I see our chancellor, as well as members of my own party, calling for substantial budget cuts. Fuel prices keep rising, driven by our dependence on fossil fuels and the problems involving Iran.
I think we are currently seeing some of the highest prices ever at petrol pumps and filling stations. At the same time, we are seeing a major increase in electric vehicle use. In Denmark, for example, electric vehicles already account for 80% of new car sales, while in Germany the figure is 30%. So I think we need to move in that direction.”
MEP Daniel Freund and BNR's Irina Nedeva in the Radio Studios complex at the European Parliament in Strasbourg (21 October 2026)
PHOTO Rositsa Petkova
Italy, Greece, Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia are preparing a petition calling for a further postponement or weakening of the emissions trading scheme. Europe must nevertheless maintain its climate targets, the politician insisted in an interview with BNR Horizon's programme “Strasbourg Calling”:
“We do not want to keep spending billions to support petrol producers, these huge companies, and in doing so also support dictators. We want to put an end to that! We want to continue transforming our economies and making them increasingly green. This summer, we saw 32,000 Europeans lose their lives during heatwaves. And yet it was the coolest summer compared with those forecast to come. So we certainly need to keep moving in this direction.”
Daniel Freund argued that decarbonisation is not incompatible with industrial competitiveness:
“We can already see what is happening in China. The Chinese market has stopped buying cars with internal combustion engines from us, and only electric vehicles are being used. The same applies to other products. So if we want to remain competitive, we need to offer the right products. For example, companies that use electric trucks and renewable energy are not currently being affected by the fuel crisis.”
Europe must strengthen its defence industry, but even defence is becoming greener, he noted:
“Even if we look at the battlefield in Ukraine, we can see that this war is being fought, to some extent, using renewable energy. A large number of drones are being deployed, and they operate on batteries. What we must do is stand together in defending Ukraine, because in doing so we are fighting for our shared values and our own survival.”
The Greens will support the European Parliament resolution aimed at strengthening security in the Black Sea in response to Russian threats, he added:
“I think we will support the resolution. We stand with Bulgaria, Romania and every country that falls victim to such Russian attacks.”
Irina Nedeva’s full interview with MEP Daniel Freund was aired on BNR's Horizon channel on October 21 and can be heard HERE.

articles.title: More Than 50 Air Defense Turrets Built Around Putin’s Residence
articles.body:
Another 16 towers for air defense systems have been built around Vladimir Putin’s residence in Valdai, Russia.
The findings were reported by Radio Liberty, based on a joint analysis of satellite imagery with OSINT researcher jembob.
The total number of air defense positions in the area has exceeded 50.
According to the investigators, Russia built 16 towers in October within a 50-kilometer radius south of the residence, on the side facing Ukraine.
The new structures form an additional outer ring of air defenses, likely intended to house Pantsir surface-to-air gun-missile systems or Tor surface-to-air missile systems.
Journalists have not yet identified new positions in the northern part of the outer ring. They may be built over the coming months.
The new air defense ring runs through the Khotilovo military airfield and the area around the Vyshny Volochyok Reservoir.
One of the towers at Khotilovo airbase was built as early as March 2026. The airfield is used for Vladimir Putin’s flights, and a dedicated railway line connects its grounds to his residence in Valdai.
Several more positions have been established on the shore of the Vyshny Volochyok Reservoir, in the middle of which lies Lisiy Island.
Russian military personnel have built a laboratory complex on the island that, according to a Radio Liberty investigation, may be linked to Russia’s biological weapons development program.
Construction of two air defense towers near the facility began in early September, around the same time the investigation into the laboratory was published.
The total number of identified air defense positions around Valdai has therefore exceeded 50. This is roughly half the number of positions established to protect Moscow and the Moscow region since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Moscow and the surrounding region have a combined population of more than 20 million, while fewer than 100,000 people live in Valdai, Valdai District, and the surrounding area within a 50-kilometer radius.
Russia began deploying additional air defense systems near Putin’s residence in early 2023. This included the reported appearance of a Pantsir-S1 system in Yashcherovo, near the residence.
Russia is also strengthening air defenses around Moscow. In July, Militarnyi reported the construction of about 24 new towers for Pantsir systems in the Russian capital region.
In June, following a Ukrainian drone attack on Moscow in May, Russia built at least seven additional towers for Pantsir systems to the north and east of the capital.

articles.title: EU extends sanctions against Jacques Baud
articles.body:
EU extends sanctions against Jacques Baud
The European Union has extended the sanctions against Jacques Baud, a former colonel in the Swiss Army General Staff, who is accused of spreading pro-Russian propaganda, until October 9, 2027. He remains subject to an asset freeze and travel restrictions.
According to official EU documents reported by the French-speaking Swiss online media outlet L’Impertinent, on October 8 the Council of the European Union renewed the sanctions regime against Russia’s “destabilising activities”, which targets 80 individuals and 20 entities.
Added to this list on December 15, 2025, the 71-year-old Brussels resident is accused of his contributions to media outlets described as pro-Russian and of spreading “conspiracy theories”. The EU Council criticises him in particular for accusing Ukraine of having orchestrated its own invasion in order to join NATO.
Initially, Brussels accused him of supporting Russian actions that “undermine or threaten the stability or security of a third country (Ukraine)”. The new text now refers to actions that “undermine democracy and threaten the stability or security of a third country”. Ukraine is no longer explicitly mentioned, and the conjunction “or” has been replaced by “and”. The specific allegations remain unchanged. The EU has not provided any justification for the rewording.
The individual concerned disputes the allegations: “I have never received a single cent from Russia,” he stated in December 2025, notably in an interview with L’Impertinent. The 71-year-old claims to base his analyses on Ukrainian and American sources and disputes, in particular, the interpretation of his statements regarding the Russian invasion. In his view, these statements referred to an interview given in 2019 by Oleksiy Arestovych, who was to become an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Baud brought a case before the General Court of the EU last March seeking the annulment of his inclusion on the list.
+ Switzerland approves 20th sanctions package against Russia
A retired colonel of the General Staff, born in Geneva, Jacques Baud worked for the Swiss secret services from 1983 to 1990, where he was responsible for analysing Warsaw Pact forces. He subsequently held various posts with the UN, notably in Sudan.
Highly critical of the EU’s and Western countries’ policies on the war in Ukraine, Baud has a large online following, particularly on YouTube, where his videos have racked up several million views.
The sanctions are having a serious impact on his daily life. Baud can no longer freely access his bank accounts, particularly to access his pension. He also claims he is unable to leave Belgium.
After several months of restrictions, a humanitarian exemption had allowed him to regain access to his Belgian account from mid-March to the end of June. Since the beginning of July, he says, the funds have once again been inaccessible. A new exemption requested at the start of May was granted by the Belgian authorities at the start of October, but by the middle of the month it had still not been implemented.

articles.title: Druze experts condemn Tom Barrack's accusations against Syrian Druze, warn of sectarian violence
articles.body:
US envoy Tom Barrack’s claims that the area between Sweida and Daraa was “the captagon manufacturing operation of the world” and that a Druze sheikh was using perceived American and Israeli backing to “persecute other Druze” have drawn criticism from the Druze community, with some Israeli experts telling The Jerusalem Post on Sunday that the remarks had led them to question his suitability for the role.
Speaking in an interview with Lebanese-Australian podcaster Mario Nawfal on Friday, Barrack alleged that Druze in the area were living off the manufacture and sale of illicit drugs.
“It’s not Israel that worries me. It’s a particular Druze sheikh who utilizes the perception of Israeli backing of some alignment with America to persecute other Druze,” Barrack said.
Although Barrack did not name the sheikh, his comments have been widely interpreted in Arab media as referring to Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri, a spiritual leader of the Druze community who has called for Israeli support and independence from Syria.
Growing calls for Syrian Druze independence
Calls for independence and Israeli support among Syria’s Druze community have grown more frequent since Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa came to power in late 2024.
Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham, the formerly designated terrorist organization led by Sharaa, has a documented history of persecuting Druze, while the sectarian massacres in July 2025 and sporadic violence since have further fueled fears of Damascus’s Islamist government.
Against this backdrop, Israeli Druze diplomat and historian Dr. Reda Mansour criticized Barrack’s remarks in a post on X/Twitter, describing his attribution of the global Captagon trade to the Druze region and his criticism of its local leadership as “highly irresponsible” and untruthful.
“By baselessly criminalizing an entire ethnic minority, these statements put the vulnerable Druze community in southern Syria at direct risk of sectarian violence and targeted jihadi attacks. Painting a minority enclave as an illicit hub paints a dangerous target on their back for extremist networks,” Mansour wrote.
“Diplomacy demands accuracy, not reckless generalizations that compromise human lives. We stand in solidarity with the Druze community in Syria.”
Concerns rise amid ongoing violence against Druze community
Mansour’s concerns come amid continued violence against the community. More than 1,300 Druze were killed in the July 2025 massacres in Sweida and surrounding villages, according to UN figures, while subsequent outbreaks of sectarian violence have continued to see civilians abducted and killed.
Civilians have also been killed in Jordanian military strikes on facilities Amman alleges are used for weapons storage and drug manufacturing. In a strike on January 18, 2024, for example, Jordan killed sisters Farah and Dima, aged three and five, along with their parents and other members of their extended family.
Dr. Mordechai Kedar, a research fellow at the Begin-Sadat Center for Strategic Studies, told the Post that Barrack’s comments and “lack of understanding” of the region have “brought a lot of damage to the whole Middle East.”
Doubting Barrack’s knowledge of the issue of Sweida or the sectarian violence, Kedar said that he thought Barrack was relying on information provided to him and not the information on the ground or from the people affected by the violence.
Jonathan Hessen, a senior fellow at the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security, added that Barrack’s remarks were not just “dismaying” because they showed a disregard for the safety and security of a community that has already been subjected to multiple massacres but because his statements were factually unfounded.
“Even when the Jordanians launched airstrikes in southern Syria, the majority of the targeted warehouses were actually in Daraa, the province south of Sweida, where the Bedouins reside,” he said.
“One warehouse was also targeted in Sweida, although I am not aware of its contents. However, those targets were provided to the Jordanians by Damascus, so there are certain aspects that need to be taken into account.”
He noted that Barrack has a pattern of minimizing the suffering of those across the Middle East where the impact would disrupt his broader plans, referencing both Barrack’s comments last week, where he insisted that the Islamic regime was “not evil,” and past commentary on Syrian violence.

articles.title: IDF kills two terrorists who funneled millions from Iran and Turkey to Hamas
articles.body:
The IDF announced Sunday that it had killed two terrorists in separate airstrikes in the Gaza Strip last week, accusing them of transferring millions of shekels from Iran and Turkey to Hamas' military wing throughout the war. According to the military, the funds were used to help the terrorist organization rebuild its military capabilities and prepare attacks against Israeli soldiers and civilians.
The first terrorist, Alaa Ibrahim Nimer Arshi, a cell commander in Hamas' military wing, was killed in an airstrike in the Gaza City area. The second, Karam Riyad Hassan Abu Butaihan, a Palestinian Islamic Jihad terrorist who helped transfer money to Hamas, was killed in the Nuseirat area in central Gaza.
According to the IDF, both men played a role in channeling funds to Hamas throughout the war, including money originating from Iran and Turkey. The military said the financial transfers had recently supported Hamas' efforts to restore its military infrastructure and advance attacks against Israeli forces and civilians.
In a separate operation last week, the IDF and Shin Bet security agency carried out an airstrike in central Gaza, destroying a weapons depot used by Hamas to store military equipment. The facility contained Kalashnikov rifles, a launcher and rockets, according to the military.
Additional terrorists killed in Gaza strikes
The announcement follows an IDF statement last week confirming the deaths of two additional terrorists in separate strikes.
One was Akram Bassam Shaaban Yassin, a senior member of Hamas' General Security apparatus in the Gaza Strip. The other was Tamer Mohammed Ibrahim al-Sabbagh, whom the military identified as a member of the terrorist cell responsible for abducting and murdering German-Israeli citizen Shani Louk during the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel.

articles.title: Russian Strike Hits Epicentr Mall in Poltava, Woman Injured
articles.body:
A Russian aerial strike struck the Epicentr shopping center in the central city of Poltava on Sunday, Oct. 25, igniting a fire across the commercial building and injuring a 52-year-old woman, regional authorities reported.
Head of the Poltava Regional Military Administration Vitalii Diakivnych announced on Telegram that incoming fire struck the large retail center, triggering an immediate blaze and causing structural damage.

“A fire broke out. Information regarding the extent of the damage is being clarified. Liquidation of the consequences of the attack is ongoing. Preliminarily, a 52-year-old woman sustained injuries,” Diakivnych stated.
Emergency responders, specialized firefighting brigades, and civil defense units deployed to the site of the hit to contain the blaze, secure the perimeter, and evaluate whether additional personnel or visitors were inside the facility during the impact.
Weekend infrastructure strikes
The kinetic impact on the Epicentr hypermarket in Poltava follows a sequence of targeted Russian strikes against commercial retail sites, logistics facilities, and public infrastructure across Ukraine over the weekend.
On Saturday evening, Russian forces struck a commercial shopping center in the Osnovianskyi district of Kharkiv, igniting a major structural blaze, alongside strikes on a construction hypermarket and industrial facilities that wounded several civilians and three emergency rescue workers during follow-on secondary strikes.
4 Killed in Synelnykove Strike, Rescuers Hit in Kharkiv
Concurrently in Dnipropetrovsk region, a strike drone hit a residential high-rise in Synelnykove, killing four civilians and wounding 13 others.
Overnight into Sunday, Russian bombardments damaged critical infrastructure and municipal utility networks across nine regions, with impacts reported at thermal power plants, electrical substations, coal mining enterprises, grain storage facilities, and a postal depot.

articles.title: Trump seeks rapprochement with Putin, while his policies could give Russia a decisive advantage in the war – Reuters
articles.body:
Trump seeks rapprochement with Putin, while his policies could give Russia a decisive advantage in the war – Reuters
Kyiv • UNN
Trump seeks rapprochement with Putin, while the US is pressuring Kyiv over strikes on Russian oil refineries. In Kyiv, there are fears of a weakening of the defense.
U.S. President Donald Trump continues his course toward rapprochement with Russian dictator Vladimir Putin, despite the war against Ukraine. At the same time, Washington's policy raises concerns that American pressure on Kyiv could weaken Ukraine's defense capabilities and give Russia a decisive advantage. This is stated in a Reuters report, writes UNN.
Details
As the agency notes, Trump has long sought to improve relations with Russia. His approach to Putin contradicts traditional principles of U.S. foreign policy, but echoes the U.S. president's fondness for personal contacts with authoritarian leaders.
One manifestation of this approach was pressure on Ukraine over its strikes against Russia's oil infrastructure. According to the Ukrainian side, U.S. representatives even warned that intelligence-sharing could be suspended if Kyiv continued attacking Russian oil refineries.
Kyiv fears that U.S. policy will strengthen Russia's position
Former U.S. official Suriya Jayanti, who worked in Ukraine's energy sector, told Reuters that she was concerned that Washington's actions could have much broader consequences than merely stopping strikes on energy facilities.
In her assessment, U.S. policy could undermine Ukraine's potential and create conditions in which Russia would gain a decisive advantage in the war.
At the same time, Reuters draws attention to Trump's special attitude toward Putin. The U.S. president has repeatedly demonstrated a willingness to move closer to the Kremlin, even when this has caused concern among U.S. allies.
