articles.title: Iran prepared for any scenario, will not succumb to threat
articles.body:
In an interview with German broadcaster ARD on Sunday, Baghaei said Iran has learned that Washington and its leadership cannot be trusted, as their strategy “is not diplomacy, but attacking the Islamic Republic.”
Responding to President Donald Trump’s rhetoric that the US will not attack Iran before the midterm elections, he emphasized that regardless of what the US president says or does not say, Iranians remain prepared, given American attacks even while diplomatic processes were underway.
He recalled a statement by Omani Foreign Minister Badr bin Hamad Al Busaidi that Iran and the US had made significant progress, yet Washington still chose to attack Iran—a reference to the American war amid talks with Oman acting as an intermediary. “The US has not shown the least bit of goodwill and will for a diplomatic approach,” Baghaei noted.
In response to a question regarding Europe’s approach toward Iran, Baghaei said it was regrettable to see the Europeans appeasing the United States rather than adopting an independent stance. The international community expects the European Union to act maturely in global politics, he added.
Consequently, the Europeans, instead of playing a constructive role regarding the nuclear issue, chose to side with the United States—despite knowing the illegality of the war launched against Iran, the US breach of the nuclear deal, JCPOA, in 2018, or following Washington in misusing the UN Security Council to re-impose sanctions.
Responding to developments around the Strait of Hormuz, the Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson said the strategic waterway “was not secure,” because the United States and Israel had exploited it to launch attacks on Iran—utilizing not only the Strait itself but also the territory and military infrastructure of several Persian Gulf states located on the opposite shore.
He emphasized that Iran has served as the guardian of this waterway for centuries but was compelled to take serious measures to safeguard its national security and territorial integrity—actions he said are lawful under international law.
Baghaei also referred to continued US intervention in the regional waters, saying CENTCOM—with the cooperation of certain regional states—has been pressuring vessels to use routes other than those specified by Iran, resulting in explosions and other incidents.
Stating that the Americans were exploiting the “southern route” to transport military equipment, he said any littoral state has the right to take necessary measures to prevent the aggressors from utilizing these waterways for military purposes.
Regarding Iran-Germany relations, Baghaei noted that Berlin must decide whether it wants to change its approach or simply appease the United States.
Germans once enjoyed a strong reputation in Iran, he said, but that standing has been tarnished since they failed to provide a convincing explanation as to why they provided the former Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein with chemical agents when he attacked Iran in the 1980s.
Baghaei also said that Germany’s support for the US-Israeli war over the past two years, 2025 and 2026, and other anti-Iran measures have impacted the good relations Tehran and Berlin enjoyed in the past.

articles.title: Canada and Europe want to reshape the global order. But whose vision will prevail?
articles.body:
Mark Carney’s pursuit of a global alliance of middle powers has a Europe problem.
Canada’s prime minister wants to help build a new world order that can counterbalance the power of the United States and China. But his vision depends on a new relationship with a Europe that doesn’t see itself as a middle power at all.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has a different vision: a Brussels-centered bloc that extends the EU’s economic and geopolitical influence, starting with Canada. The idea, according to senior European lawmaker Siegfried Mureșan, is to create an opportunity for the EU to become the “global center of gravity for liberal democracies.”
Advertisement
The competing visions will be tested this week when Carney and von der Leyen meet in Montreal for a summit intended to chart a new course for transatlantic relations. Both want to demonstrate they can prosper in a world upended by U.S. President Donald Trump. But they have different ideas about their curious new alliance — and face political resistance that could limit how far the partnership can go.
Von der Leyen’s offer of “associate membership” in the EU surprised officials on both sides of the Atlantic. Four diplomats told POLITICO they were not consulted before she floated the idea in the State of the Union. The officials added that they don’t understand the label, which has yet to be defined. Germany has since led pushback on the plan.
“We’ve definitely put the cart before the horse,” one of the diplomats said. “We’re announcing something and then figuring out how to flesh it out.”
Trump called the membership idea “laughable,” but also threatened “very serious tariffs” should it come to be — a reminder that leaders in pursuit of Washington workarounds must avoid provoking the White House.
The leaders are under pressure to leave Montreal with more than a liberal democratic photo-op. For starters, they need to decide what “associate membership” means — and disarm resistance in the EU capitals blindsided by von der Leyen’s plan.
Canada’s Ambassador to the EU Jonathan Wilkinson told POLITICO last month that people got too hung up on a label that was revealed prematurely. Carney called the Canada-EU relationship an “alliance for the future” when he addressed European lawmakers in Strasbourg.
Advertisement
Wilkinson said the Canada-EU project will show other democratic nations how to deepen partnerships. “It ties into very much what [Carney] talked about at Davos — and after Davos.”
Carney, von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa have two days to chart what’s next while American foreign policy continues to stress test geopolitical relationships in midterm campaigns that will shape Trump’s last two years in office.
The economic divide
Ottawa considers the EU an obvious partner in its push to diversify trade away from the U.S. There’s already a free-trade agreement that both sides view as being underutilized.
Leaders gathering in Montreal this week will celebrate the 10th anniversary of the Canadian-EU trade agreement, nicknamed CETA. But nine EU member countries have yet to ratify the deal, underscoring the challenge of turning rhetoric into reality.
“We have shared challenges and many more shared opportunities,” Canadian International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu told reporters last week in Dublin, where he was invited to participate in an informal meeting of EU trade ministers, a preview of what a more integrated Canada could look like. “Canada wants to be Europe’s most reliable partner.”
Sidhu said CETA utilization rates in EU member countries range from 60% to 80%, making a point about room for improvement and perennial challenges. “We know there’s room to grow.”
Advertisement
Von der Leyen’s associate membership plan “has been coldly received by member states,” a senior EU official said. “It [the summit] is more about what we do, how we can use the real potential of the CETA agreement.” CETAhas been provisionally in force since 2017.
Trade talks between Canada and the bloc read like a lengthy transatlantic grievance list.
At a meeting between Brussels and Ottawa last October, the EU complained about Canadian taxes it says disproportionately hit European carmakers, opaque cheese-import quotas, cumbersome rules on cosmetics and what it considers discriminatory provincial taxes and markups on European wines and spirits.
Canada, meanwhile, warned that the EU’s deforestation rules could burden its exporters, questioned the impact of Brussels’ carbon border tax and pressed for greater recognition of Canadian standards in areas including AI.
The senior EU official described the relationship as constrained by “irritants and unfulfilled promises” that must be resolved if the two sides are to make progress.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, next to European Parliament President Roberta Metsola, in Strasbourg, eastern France, on September 17, 2026. | Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/ AFP via Getty Images
There are hurdles ahead. Even as Canada and the EU imagine a deeper economic and security partnership, both are pursuing industrial policies that could shut the other’s companies out of lucrative public contracts — death by compounded trade barriers.
Advertisement
Brussels has concerns about Ottawa’s “Buy Canadian” initiatives and their compatibility with the EU-Canada free trade agreement. “Some member states didn’t like the ‘Buy Canada’ thing from Carney,” the official added.
Canada is likewise uncertain whether its companies will qualify for the EU’s proposed “Made in Europe” preferences foreseen in a major industry bill that would seek to channel public procurement spending to European companies. The EU is divided over whether to extend those preferences to trusted trading partners, a topic that is expected to come up in Montreal.
Canadian business leaders recognize the domestic appeal of “Buy Canadian” in the face of Trump’s threats, but warn there will need to be concessions.
“It’s something that will have to be resolved in order to move the relationship deeper, particularly with respect to industrial cooperation or collaboration,” Mark Camilleri, president of the Canada EU Trade and Investment Association, told POLITICO.
Camilleri likened the 10-year-old CETA deal to a garden overgrown with weeds. “It pains me to see market access being eroded through Canadian and European preferences,” he said.
Pressure is on
European and Canadian leaders are under pressure to deliver wins this week that demonstrate that “non-hegemons” — a descriptor Carney used in his Davos speech — can survive and thrive in an age of great-power rivalry.
Advertisement
Canadians currently support closer ties with Europe. But the EU faces political headwinds of its own, from fraught budget negotiations within the bloc to right-wing populist movements that are picking up momentum in some of its biggest economies.
One likely deliverable is a new digital trade agreement. Talks launched in March and were still underway last week. But the agreement lacks substantive text on artificial intelligence, leaving the two sides to find other places to cooperate, potentially through the EU’s proposed Cloud and AI Development Act. That proposal seeks to reduce reliance on U.S. tech giants, raising the risk of a new row with Washington.
The European Commission is also pushing for Canada to join Erasmus+, the bloc’s student exchange program, according to one EU official. Carney has already publicly expressed interest.
But Brussels has bigger ambitions for the partnership. The EU is pressing Canada to increase its funding for Ukraine, a test of Canada’s willingness to take on more of the security burden.
For von der Leyen, securing that commitment would be a win. So would leaving the summit with a pledge from Carney to explore her offer of an “associate membership” — or whatever they end up calling it.
Zi-Ann Lum reported from Toronto, Sebastian Starcevic from Brussels and Camille Gijs from Dublin.

articles.title: Royal Canadian Air Force Receives First Two CF-35A Fighter Jets
articles.body:
The Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF) has received its first two CF-35A fifth-generation fighter jets at Luke Air Force Base in Arizona.
The RCAF announced the delivery on its official X account.
The first eight aircraft will be based at Luke Air Force Base, where Canadian pilots will receive training to operate the F-35A fighter jets.
The first aircraft are expected to arrive in Canada in 2028, once the Department of National Defence has completed the necessary infrastructure to receive them.
Canada joined the F-35 program in 2002 as a Tier 3 partner. This was the lowest of the three partnership levels in terms of financial contribution during the aircraft’s development and testing phase. Canada committed approximately $150 million to the program.
In return, Canadian companies gained opportunities to manufacture F-35 parts. These include airframe components, horizontal stabilizers, wing sections, landing gear parts, and engine sensors.
According to Canada’s Department of National Defence, 37 Canadian companies currently hold contracts under the F-35 program. Canadian-made components are worth an estimated $2.2 million per aircraft. More than 110 Canadian companies have received contracts related to the program, worth a combined total of over $ 3.6 billion.
However, Canada did not make its final decision to select the F-35A (CF-35A) over its competitor, the Swedish Saab Gripen E, to replace its CF-188 Hornet fighters until 2022. In January 2023, the Canadian government signed an agreement to purchase 88 aircraft.
The situation changed after Donald Trump returned to power and launched a trade war. On March 14, 2025, just days after taking office as prime minister, Mark Carney ordered a review of the decision to purchase 88 F-35A fighters.
In May 2026, Canada’s Department of National Defence said the review was still underway and that a final decision would be announced at a later date. Meanwhile, preparations to receive the F-35s are continuing.
In late September, the first F-35A fighter jet designated for the Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF), locally known as theCF-35A, made its maiden flight.
The aircraft, bearing manufacturer serial number AR-1, took off on September 23, 2026, from Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth in Texas, where Lockheed Martin’s production facility is located.

articles.title: Iran fully united, on highest alert amid US-Israeli threats: official
articles.body:
Iran fully united, on highest alert amid US-Israeli threats: official
TEHRAN— Iran remains fully united and on the highest level of alert amid continuing threats from the United States and Israel, Saeed Khatibzadeh, head of the Foreign Ministry’s Center for Political and International Studies, has said, warning that any further US military action would lead to another failure.
Speaking to reporters on Sunday on the sidelines of the inauguration of the Martyr Kamal Kharrazi Documentation Center and Museum in Tehran, Khatibzadeh emphasized Iran’s national unity and readiness to respond to threats against its security.
He said Europe had made a series of misguided decisions in recent months and was now facing the consequences of its own policies, adding that European countries had marginalized themselves on major international issues through their approach to regional developments.
Khatibzadeh called on European governments to distance themselves from the Israeli regime’s actions and repeated violations of international and humanitarian law.
He stressed that confidence in European countries would remain difficult to establish unless they explicitly condemned such actions, stopped allowing the United States to use their military bases, and demonstrated a genuine commitment to upholding international law.
The Iranian official also warned Washington against further military action, saying that if the first and second wars against Iran had failed to achieve their objectives, another military campaign would prove equally unsuccessful.
He stressed that efforts should instead focus on building a peaceful Iran and a stable region, free from 'the destabilizing presence of the United States and its allies.'
Khatibzadeh condemns attack on Foreign Ministry library
In separate remarks at the inauguration ceremony, Khatibzadeh condemned the Israeli attack on the Foreign Ministry’s specialized library, saying the strike had disrupted the activities of the century-old institution for the first time in its history.
Comparing the attack to the destruction caused by the Mongol invasions, he described the library as one of Iran’s leading specialized academic resources in foreign policy, international economics, international relations and international law. The collection contains Iranian and foreign publications in multiple languages.
The ceremony marked the inauguration of the Documentation Center and Museum dedicated to Seyyed Kamal Kharrazi, a prominent Iranian diplomat and former foreign minister who died on April 9, 2026, from injuries sustained in a US-Israeli airstrike on his Tehran residence on April 1.

articles.title: Iraq braces for renewed Iran conflict after 1,000 strikes on Kurdistan, 600 militia attacks
articles.body:
Iraq is on edge over the prospect of renewed fighting with Iran after Tehran carried out some 1,000 strikes on the Kurdistan Region in northern Iraq. Additionally, Iranian-backed militias launched roughly 600 attacks inside Iraq, most of them on US diplomatic facilities.
Iraq closed some border crossings with Iran, including the Al-Sheeb crossing in southern Iraq, on Wednesday, saying it needed upgrades to security and technical infrastructure. Iran criticized the decision, saying Baghdad failed to provide advance notice and rejected allegations that narcotics and counterfeit currency are being smuggled into Iraq through border crossings, according to a Rudaw report.
This crossing, also known as Al-Shaib, was the first targeted for closure in Maysan Governorate. This crossing is believed to be near an area where an Iranian-backed militia in Iraq launched a drone strike on Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline in September. Rudaw also reported that, in retaliation, Iranian businessman Babak Zanjani called for restrictions on Iraqi oil tankers passing through the Strait of Hormuz.
Meanwhile, the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) has denied reports that Ukrainian forces, military units or drones are operating from its territory. The KRG Interior Ministry issued a statement on Thursday rejecting the allegations as baseless, according to the Iraqi News Agency (INA). However, the source of the reports remains unclear.
The ministry emphasized that the Kurdistan region maintains a policy of neutrality in regional and international conflicts. It said it would not allow its territory to serve as a base for hostile military operations against other countries. The statement reflects the KRG's efforts to avoid being sucked into conflicts involving Iran, as Tehran has been pressuring Iraq to expel Kurdish-Iranian opposition groups that are present in the Kurdistan region of northern Iraq.
Iraq, Jordan move to strengthen bilateral security
In another development, Iraq and Jordan have emphasized the importance of strengthening bilateral security cooperation. According to the Iraqi News Agency (INA), Iraqi Interior Minister Yasser al-Maliki spoke by telephone on Wednesday with his Jordanian counterpart, Mazen al-Faraya. Faraya congratulated Maliki on assuming his new position, and the two officials discussed expanding coordination between their interior ministries.
The Iraqi Interior Ministry said the conversation reflected the two countries' commitment to strengthening security and stability through closer cooperation. The discussion comes as Baghdad seeks to manage security along its borders. While Jordan and Iraq have positive historic ties, the desert area near Jordan and Syria in Iraq’s Western Anbar area has been a source of threats in the past. This is a largely tribal, sparsely populated area that could become a security vacuum following the US withdrawal from Iraq and Syria.
Iraq is also focusing on security along its western border with Syria. According to the Iraqi News Agency (INA), Defense Minister Nayef Mukayif al-Shammari conducted an aerial inspection tour on Saturday of Iraqi military units deployed along the Iraq-Syria border in Nineveh province. The Iraqi Defense Ministry said the visit aimed to review force deployment and positioning along the border and assess operational readiness.

articles.title: Rubio describes Russia-Ukraine war as territorial dispute ahead of November peace talks
articles.body:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio appeared to reduce Russia’s invasion of Ukraine to a territorial dispute over the Donbas Region in comments to reporters last week.
"(P)eople keep talking about it's a war in Ukraine. That war is about Donbas. It's about one region of the country," Rubio told reporters during a visit to India last week.
"At its core, (the war) is about 11% of one part of that country that Russia wants and cannot take militarily and that Ukraine is unwilling to give up."
This comes after the US announced that trilateral peace talks between the three countries would take place in November.
In a major departure from US foreign policy, President Donald Trump waived sanctions for Russia and announced that the US would be purchasing Russian diesel.
Does the US understand what is going on in Ukraine?
But by framing the Ukraine-Russia War as a territorial dispute, Rubio’s comments could reveal where the Trump administration’s head is at before the talks in November.
It also signals that the administration has a profound misunderstanding of the war and Putin’s ambitions for Ukraine.
Putin said on Thursday that the territories in eastern Ukraine claimed by Moscow were "historically Russian land," raising stakes in talks to settle the conflict.
"Firstly, my attitude on this matter is that this is not their territory. It’s the territory of historical Russia," he said.
Putin also said any future trilateral talks involving Russia, the United States and Ukraine should focus on security guarantees for both Russia and Ukraine, adding that broader European security issues should also be discussed.
"The goal of these talks will be to ensure the security of Ukraine and Russia after reaching peace agreements, in their final form, not as a result of a temporary ceasefire for some short period of time. We are ready to resume these contacts to achieve this goal," Putin said.
The Russian president said Witkoff also stressed that discussions had to extend to "the architecture of European security as a whole. And I agree with that too. Well, let's see how things develop in the coming days."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who met Witkoff in Norway on Tuesday, said Ukraine was ready for talks likely to take place by early next month. Ukraine, he said, supported "any proposals for a ceasefire, an end to the war, an energy ceasefire as well as humanitarian initiatives."

articles.title: BSF apprehends four Pakistani fishermen in Kutch, seizes boat
articles.body:
The Border Security Force (BSF) has apprehended four Pakistani fishermen who allegedly entered Indian waters for crab-catching activities and seized a fishing boat near the India-Pakistan border in Gujarat’s Kutch district.According to news agency PTI, the fishermen were apprehended from the Sir Creek area on Sunday following specific intelligence inputs, an official said. The fishermen were identified as Kadir Thaimor, Muhammad Mussa, Azgar Thaimor and Ahsan Jat, all residents of Chach Jaan Khan village in Pakistan’s Sindh province, according to information provided by the BSF.Sir Creek is a narrow, marshy tidal channel in the Rann of Kutch, along the coastal region between Gujarat and Pakistan’s Sindh province. The area is strategically sensitive because the longstanding India-Pakistan boundary dispute over the creek affects the demarcation of the maritime boundary in the Arabian Sea.The region’s shallow waters, tidal channels and extensive marshlands make navigation and border surveillance challenging. Fishing activities in the area can also lead to fishermen crossing into the other country’s waters, prompting apprehensions by security personnel.
The BSF maintains surveillance along the sensitive western border to prevent unauthorised crossings and other illegal activities. The latest apprehension follows an operation based on specific intelligence inputs, during which the four fishermen and their boat were taken into custody.
Aryan Singh is a journalist with The Times of India, covering breaking news, defence and global conflicts. An alumnus of the IIMC, he tracks the people, weapons and geopolitics behind the headlines, with a focus on India’s national security, military affairs and conflicts shaping the world.

articles.title: From lawyer's office to kitchen: dad of American soldier killed in Ukraine volunteers in Kharkiv
articles.body:
From lawyer's office to kitchen: dad of American soldier killed in Ukraine volunteers in Kharkiv
Edward Wilton's son was killed serving in Ukraine's International Legion. Now Edward has moved to Kharkiv to help civilians. Every day he helps prepare hot meals for local residents, including hospital patients.
Source: Independence Avenue Media
Details: For most of his adult life, Edward Wilton practised law in Florida. But after the death of his son, who served as a volunteer in the International Legion, Edward came to help Ukraine too.
In January 2026, Edward retired and moved to Kharkiv for good. Now he works at the Pekelna Kuhnya (Hell's Kitchen) charity alongside many other volunteers from around the world – the United Kingdom, Poland, Japan, Sweden and other countries.
Every day they prepare more than 1,200 meals for local residents, most of which are delivered to the city's hospitals.
Quote from Edward: "I returned to help Ukraine and to help out what I think is my country too."
Details: Edward said he does his best to be useful, adding that he adores Kharkiv and loves Ukraine and its people. He thinks it is an incredible place to live – a place he now calls home.
In an earlier report, Edward told Suspilne Ivano-Frankivsk that he has Ukrainian roots. He said his mother had always told him that she was Ukrainian, Polish or Austrian, and that this uncertainty prompted him to research his family history.
Eventually Edward discovered that his great-grandfather came from Kosmach, a Hutsul village in the Prykarpattia region, and emigrated to the US in 1912 or 1913. Edward raised his son, Edward III, with an awareness of his Ukrainian heritage and in the spirit of Ukrainian traditions.
Edward said his family had preserved some traditions that were passed down through his mother's family, particularly around celebrating Christmas and Easter, and had talked a lot about their ancestors' heritage.
Edward III had always wanted to become a soldier. He was unable to complete his military training in the US, but spent several months training to become an emergency medical technician.
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion, Edward III travelled to Ukraine and joined the International Legion. He served in the Bravo Company under the alias "Hans" and took part in complex combat operations, for which he was awarded the Order of Courage.
Edward said his son had trained with various weapons, studied tactics with his unit and was very proficient with a grenade launcher. He added that Edward III was one of the youngest in his unit and that his brothers-in-arms perhaps had more combat experience than he did.
Edward said his son had not said anything about returning home before the war was over: everything was connected to the war. His son had had several opportunities to return home but had refused, saying he had not yet earned that right; he believed he needed to do more than he was doing.
Edward said his son was fascinated by Ukraine and did not want to return to the US.
Edward III died in April 2023 from a shrapnel wound, aged 22. He and his brothers-in-arms had come under artillery fire while moving out to positions in Luhansk Oblast.
Edward said his son really wanted to be in control of his own life. He recalled reading the Iliad with him when his son was a child, including the passage about Achilles, who had to choose between a long, uneventful life and a short, heroic one. Edward said his son had told him even then that he wanted a short, heroic life rather than a long, boring one, and added that that is exactly what happened.
A memorial in honour of the fighter now stands in Kosmach – the village that his father now regards as his home. Since losing his son, Edward has treasured the certificate presented to him for his service.
"My son said he didn't mind dying, but he wanted to be remembered," he said.

articles.title: Dutch Army Plans to Replace Kodiak Engineer Vehicles After Just 12 Years in Service
articles.body:
The Dutch Ministry of Defense plans to replace its Kodiak engineer vehicles and, in cooperation with Germany, acquire additional Leguan tank-launched bridges.
The Dutch Ministry of Defense outlined the plans in an official letter to parliament dated October 22, 2026.
The Dutch Army has operated Kodiak engineer vehicles since 2014. They are designed for engineering tasks, mine clearance, breaching obstacles, and creating passages for military vehicles.
However, the Ministry of Defense considers the vehicles outdated because their protection no longer meets today’s battlefield threats. The vehicles also have low operational availability because individual systems and components malfunction.
The military initially considered upgrading the Kodiaks under a Midlife Update (MLU) program but abandoned the option because of its technical complexity and lengthy implementation timeline.
The ministry emphasized that the war in Ukraine has shown the need for modern capabilities to overcome engineering obstacles directly in combat.
The replacement and expansion program has been allocated a budget range of €250 million to €1 billion in 2026 prices, including a risk reserve.
The Ministry of Defense plans to complete the study and procurement preparation phase in the first half of 2028, after which it will present further plans to parliament. The type of replacement engineer vehicle has not yet been determined.
In October, Militarnyi reported the start of trials of two Pionierpanzer 3 Kodiak engineer vehicles in Germany. German troops received them without the Natter remotely operated weapon stations originally planned for installation.
The AEV 3 Kodiak is an armored engineer vehicle developed by Germany’s Rheinmetall in cooperation with Switzerland’s RUAG, based on the Leopard 2 tank chassis.
It is designed to clear paths through minefields, breach engineering obstacles, prepare defensive positions, and perform earthmoving tasks. In 2014, the Netherlands received 10 vehicles for its engineer units.
The Kodiak weighs about 62 tons and is equipped with a front-mounted excavator arm, a bulldozer blade, and two winches.
The blade can be replaced with a specialized mine plow to clear paths through minefields.
The Dutch Ministry of Defense also plans to procure additional Leguan tank-launched bridges to strengthen its engineer units.
To do so, the Netherlands intends to join Germany’s contract for modernized Leguan bridge-layers. Germany is expected to sign the relevant agreement with a German supplier in the first quarter of 2027.
The additional bridge-layers have been allocated a budget range of €50 million to €250 million in 2026 prices, including a risk reserve. The exact number of vehicles has not been disclosed.
The Leguan, manufactured by KNDS, is designed to rapidly deploy bridges across water obstacles and dry gaps. The system, mounted on a Leopard 2 chassis, can deploy either a single 26-meter bridge or two 14-meter bridges.
In January, Belgium signed a contract with KNDS to order eight wheeled Leguan bridge-layers worth approximately €80 million.
In February, it was also reported that the Netherlands planned to acquire WiSENT 2 armored recovery vehicles to equip new units.

articles.title: Explosion rocks Yemen's Aden as suspected Houthi missile lands near military headquarters
articles.body:
Shukri Hussein and Rania Abushamala
25 October 2026•Update: 25 October 2026
A powerful explosion rocked Yemen's southern Aden governorate Sunday after a suspected Houthi ballistic missile landed near a government military headquarters, a local source told Anadolu.
The missile landed in a remote sandy area in Bir Ahmed, behind an iron factory in the Al-Buraiqa district of western Aden, said the source, who requested anonymity.
No casualties or material damage were reported, the source added.
There was no immediate official comment from the Yemeni government or its military forces.
Aden serves as the interim capital of Yemen's internationally recognized government, which controls large parts of the country's southern and eastern provinces.
The Houthis control the capital Sanaa and much of northern and western Yemen.

articles.title: Netanyahu shares AI-generated image of nuclear explosion in Tel Aviv, two days before election
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu shared an AI-generated image depicting a nuclear explosion over Tel Aviv on Sunday, just two days before Israel's October 27 election, prompting criticism from opposition leaders who accused him of attempting to frighten voters ahead of the polls.
The image, posted on Netanyahu's official Instagram account, shows a massive mushroom cloud rising over a densely populated city, with an enormous explosion engulfing the buildings beneath it.
Accompanying the image, Netanyahu warned that Israel faced an existential threat from Iran and that the country's security depended on the outcome of Tuesday's election.
"The State of Israel is in existential danger that Iran and its proxies threaten us with. It is astonishing that nothing has changed, and more than that, everything has become more dangerous because of the existential danger posed by Iran and the axis of evil," he shared.
Netanyahu added that the developments and new findings required the public to "put aside the disputes and think only about the most important issue: ending the work in Iran."
The post did not explicitly identify the city in the image, though it appeared to show Tel Aviv.
Golan calls for Netanyahu to be kept off social media
Democrats chairman Yair Golan responded to the image on X, accusing Netanyahu and those around him of losing control as election day approached.
"The prime minister of Israel published an image of an atomic bomb over Tel Aviv," Golan wrote. "I ask that he be kept away from social media. The man and those around him have lost it. The pressure is mounting."
"On Tuesday, we will replace those spreading panic and restore security and sanity to Israel," he added.
Golan's response came amid a broader dispute over Netanyahu's handling of the Iranian threat, which has become a central issue in the final days of the election campaign.
Eisenkot accuses Netanyahu of using fear to win votes
Yashar chairman Gadi Eisenkot also condemned the publication, accusing Netanyahu of resorting to familiar election tactics.
"Another fearmongering video from Netanyahu," Eisenkot wrote. "You are hysterical. As in every election campaign, once again the same method of lies and fearmongering."
Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of threatening Israelis with mass destruction after, he claimed, failing to achieve the objectives of the war against Iran.
"You have failed. In two days, the people of Israel will show you that at the ballot box," Eisenkot wrote.

articles.title: Royal Navy moves to buy U.S.-made Skydio X10D drones
articles.body:
- Britain’s Ministry of Defence opened a tender for Skydio X10D reconnaissance drones with an estimated value of about $160,700 excluding VAT.
- Bids are due Nov. 19, and the contract is set to run until March 31, 2027.
Britain’s Ministry of Defence has opened a tender to buy Skydio X10D small drones, the American-made reconnaissance quadcopter already ordered by the thousands by the U.S. Army, with an estimated budget of £120,000 (about $160,700) excluding VAT, according to a notice on the Defence Sourcing Portal.
The tender was issued by Navy Commercial, the Royal Navy’s procurement office at Whale Island in Portsmouth, and published on Oct. 20 under the Procurement Act 2023. It does not say how many drones the ministry plans to buy or which unit will operate them. Delivery is listed for the South-East of England.
The contract is short. Bids are due by Nov. 19, the ministry expects to pick a supplier around Nov. 26, and the formal notice lists the contract as running from Nov. 30, 2026, to March 31, 2027, the end of the British government’s financial year. The listing on the Defence Sourcing Portal gives a slightly later start date of Dec. 10. The tender is open to any qualifying supplier, is marked as suitable for small and medium-sized businesses, and will be decided on price.
The X10D is a compact, rucksack-portable quadcopter built by Skydio in Hayward, California, for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance. It carries day and thermal cameras, uses onboard artificial intelligence to fly itself around obstacles, including in complete darkness, and can track a subject day or night. The drone can switch radio channels automatically to keep its link under jamming and is designed to hold its position without relying on GPS.
The X10D has been on the U.S. Department of War’s Blue UAS list of drones cleared for military use since May 2024. In March, the U.S. Army ordered more than 2,500 X10Ds for over $52 million, the largest single-vendor small drone order in Army history. Spain awarded a contract worth up to €18 million (about $18.7 million) for the drone in February 2025, and Norway followed with an initial tender worth 101 million Norwegian kroner (about $9.4 million) in July 2025.
The UK Ministry of Defence already has experience with Skydio. In May 2022, Defence Equipment and Support’s Future Capabilities Group awarded a contract worth about £3 million (about $3.8 million) for the company’s earlier X2D drone, delivered with British partner Marlborough Communications, after buying and testing 90 Skydio drones in 2020.

articles.title: Preparations Underway for Putin-Trump-Xi Trilateral Summit, Ushakov Says
articles.body:
Preparations have commenced for a trilateral summit bringing together Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov announced on Sunday, Oct. 25.
Speaking to Russian state television network Vesti and reported by news outlet Astra, Ushakov confirmed that Moscow, Beijing, and Washington have agreed in principle to convene the three-way leader-level meeting.

“Right now, I can already state definitely that Moscow, Beijing, and Washington are in principle ready to hold it, and preparations for it have already begun,” Ushakov said.
The senior Kremlin aide indicated that the trilateral summit is being planned to take place on the sidelines of the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ summit scheduled for Nov. 18–19 in Shenzhen, China.
Addressing parallel diplomatic tracks, Ushakov characterized a prospective three-way meeting involving delegations from the Russia, the US and Ukraine in November as exploratory in nature, describing it as having a “range-finding character.”
APEC summit and conditions for Miami G20 attendance
Ushakov also addressed the possibility of Vladimir Putin attending the Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami, Florida, scheduled for December, confirming that the Kremlin has received a formal invitation to the gathering from Washington.
However, the aide stated that Putin’s prospective travel to the US remains contingent upon the operational progress and concrete diplomatic outcomes achieved during the November APEC meetings in Shenzhen.
Trump Eyes Post-War Business Ties With Both Ukraine and Russia
“For now, we are discussing the November summit in Shenzhen, but we have received an invitation,” Ushakov stated regarding the Miami G20 invitation.
Asked directly whether the decision regarding Putin’s travel to Florida depends significantly on the success of the trilateral summit in China, Ushakov answered affirmatively.
“Of course. But as I say: first comes November, and then comes December,” Ushakov emphasized, underscoring that diplomatic sequencing will dictate Moscow’s scheduling determinations.
Diplomatic controversy and international legal hurdles
The prospect of direct leader-level engagements involving Trump, Putin, and Xi unfolds amid acute sensitivity across European capitals regarding great-power diplomacy brokered without the direct participation of affected European partners and Ukraine.
Former Ukrainian Prime Minister Arseniy Yatsenyuk cautioned on Saturday that three-way arrangements between Washington, Moscow, and Beijing risk partitioning European security architectures, comparing prospective summitry without Ukraine to the 1938 Munich Agreement and the 1945 Yalta Conference.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has consistently stressed that no diplomatic architecture affecting Ukraine’s sovereignty or borders can be concluded over Kyiv’s head.
The Kremlin’s confirmation of the Miami invitation also intersects with institutional pushback from EU officials and international legal bodies.
EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas and the European Commission have repeatedly criticized White House overtures toward the Russian head of state, citing state-sponsored hybrid sabotage operations across Europe and an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague charging Putin with war crimes connected to the unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children.
